Part 3 of the M1a stack (#52, a milestone of #51), split out of #68 so each PR's checks (coverage of changed lines, mutation) run on its own lines. Base: `feat/radiant-map-2-tools` (#72). Merge bottom-up, each only with the owner's go-ahead; before merging a base with `--delete-branch`, retarget the PR above it to `main`, or GitHub closes it. Draft.

The agent edits the map open in the user's Radiant through the t7_radiant_bridge plugin (McReaper/t7_radiant_bridge#3).

## Texturing and copies

- `map_edit`'s `texture` op lays a material face by face: `faces` (top, bottom, sides, or directions such as `+x,-y`), `tile` (world units one repeat spans), `scale`, `origin` (where tiles start, so faces that meet run on without a seam), `fit` (repeats across each face, from its edge: `[0, 1]` for a trim), `rotate`, `flip`. `copy` repeats entities and world brushes by a step, `count` times. `@n` names what op n of the batch made, every copy included, so a room built, textured and copied is one undo step.
- The face format was read off Radiant's own Fit Texture on a test box at 0, 90 and 30 degrees: a face's texture is projected along the world axis its normal is closest to, its W and H the world units one repeat spans, its offsets world units. Two tests replay those fits (they fail on a flipped wall axis or a backwards rotation); at 30°, Radiant's Fit sizes v along the face's bounding box's diagonal, which the turned axes give back exactly.
- A material's default tile, for texture ops and every new box (64 before), is the size the install's maps use it at most, read from every face of `map_source` (about a second, once per install): `script_wall` at 128 on 993 of its 1,042 faces, the dirty red brick at 64 on 2,083 of 2,122. A material used on fewer than 10 faces gets its GDT's tiling at 16 texels a unit (`gdt.MaterialTiling`: `tilingWidth`/`tilingHeight`, or the largest image after `mipBase` for `<auto>`), the density stock maps give 79 of the 96 often-used materials with a set tiling. The answer gives each material's tile and where it came from.
- Live: one batch of eleven ops (a plank floor, four brick walls caulked top and bottom through `@1`–`@4`, a riveted baseboard fitted to its height, a concrete pillar copied three times, a light) landed as one undo step, every op found back; a fullbright shot from inside showed each material at the scale stock maps have it. The template's volumes (fpstool, start zone, sun, umbra, over ±1536) draw their tool textures over a shot from inside them; `map_view`'s `hide volumes` now hides every volume and trigger for one shot (`View/Hide Entities/Hide Selected`, then `View/Show Last Hidden`, which shows only what it hid).
- `map_view` refuses a capture all one colour: later in the same session every capture came back pure white while the bridge answered as usual, Windows having stopped drawing the window (`PrintWindow`'s full-content mode reads what it composes); an agent got a white image it would have read as a map.

## Finding materials

- `map_materials` / `t7kb map materials` lists the materials Radiant's texture browser shows (a `usage` other than `<not in editor>`): by usage (the browser's filter: floor, interior wall, exterior trim…), surface (the `surfaceType`) and name words, the ones the install's maps use most first, each with its tile as `map_edit` lays it. On the install: 6,832 such materials of 67,114; 112 brick walls, `t7_brick_worn_dirty_red_wet` first at 2,122 faces. Materials marked DO NOT USE, which Radiant crosses out (`script_wall` among them), come only with `all`.
- The GDT index keeps a material's `usage`, `surfaceType`, `colorMap` and `doNotUse` lines beside its header, so the catalog needs no parse (2,004 GDTs, 9 s): 0.5 s warm. The index cache's version goes to 3, rebuilt once.
- `show` lays the first 16 out in the user's Radiant: a slab each, at its tile, in rows above the map, framed from straight above, fullbright, volumes hidden, then undone (the edit's own undo entry, else a delete). The answer's `board` says which label is which material. Tested on the fake (which now undoes edits), and live (below).

## Rooms in one op (part 4 replaces it with the layout op)

- `map_edit`'s `room` op builds a room around its inside box, to Treyarch's scale standards by default: floor and ceiling slabs over the walls' footprint, a wall on each side not `open` (a corridor is open at its ends), doors and windows (`holes`: side, position along the wall, width, height, sill) left as holes the walls are built around, as CSG Subtract would carve the map's volumes. The faces its pieces hide of each other are caulk, found by `map_check`'s own geometry.
- Live, on a copy of the template: a room with a door and a window landed as one undo step, 11 pieces and a light; `map_check` on its pieces found nothing; a fullbright shot from inside showed the brick running on across the pieces around both holes, the plank floor and the plaster ceiling. As one op it costs 76 tokens to write, against 254 for the boxes one by one.
- `map_materials`' board, seen live: framed from the lens on its rectangle, centred despite its one-degree tilt (straight down, Radiant drops the yaw and the board came out turned), each slab numbered 1–16 in its corner.

## Checking the texturing

- `map_check` / `t7kb map check` lists, the worst kinds first: materials no GDT defines; seams (one material's faces on one plane, both seen, sharing an edge, whose tiles differ); stretched tiles; and drawn faces nothing can see (against an opaque brush's face, or inside an opaque brush), which should be caulk. Each by brush id and face, as `map_edit`'s texture op takes them.
- Whether a material draws comes from its `materialType` (caulk `tools_replace`, clip `tools_blend`; the `script_` blockout textures are `lit` though filed under usage `tools`), kept in the index's catalog fields.
- Oracle on the stock prefabs (637 prefabs, 117,778 world faces, 56% tool materials): 85% of the faces it calls hi

## What was missing

Part of #9 (shader and techset authoring): decompiling a Black Ops III shader to HLSL in one MCP call, to start a custom shader from a stock one. The mod tools ship the compiled shaders but not their sources.

## The change

A new tool, `shader_decompile` (and `t7kb shader decompile`), on top of [t7_dxbc](https://github.com/McReaper/t7_dxbc), the decompiler now published as its own repository with its own oracles.

- `name` is a file of the mod tools' shader cache (`share/assetconvert/shaders/pc/v7`), a shader source (`techsetdef_unlit.hlsl`) or a material type (`emissive_add`, whose techset gives its in-game source).
- The cache's hash covers the source's content and defines, and the stock sources aren't shipped, so it can't be recomputed: a source's permutations are grouped by the program they compiled to instead (code, signatures, reflection). With one program for the stage, the answer is its HLSL in one call; with several, what each reads ($Globals, textures and buffers, inputs), plus a material type's techset constants, to pick one by name.
- The HLSL compiles back to the same shader with the names a techset binds by: entry point `ps_main`/`vs_main`, material parameters as global variables. Long HLSL comes a page at a time, as `get` serves documents.
- `internal/shader` holds the cache's rules; `CLAUDE.md` and the README list the tool. The skill that teaches the custom-shader workflow comes in the next PR.

## How it was verified

- **In game** (`zm_rainy_d2om`): `emissive_add`'s pixel shader, decompiled and used through a custom techset with the stock vertex shader, rendered like the stock material on a panel beside it; a demo effect added on top (time from `gameTime.w`, distance from `SV_Position.w`) showed as written. The install was restored and checked by hashes afterwards.
- On the real install: `emissive_add` gives `techsetdef_unlit.hlsl`'s three pixel-shader programs, twelve permutations each, the one reading `colorTint` among them; a cache file decompiles in one call with `alike: 11`; `deferred_lighting.hlsl` groups its 1,176 permutations.
- Tests run on a miniature cache of shaders compiled from t7_dxbc's own test HLSL (no game content): 98–100 % of the new code covered; the tool over MCP, the CLI, paging, every error path.
- Mutation testing (go-mutesting, 78 + 114 mutants of `internal/shader/shader.go` and `internal/cli/shader_ops.go`): every mutant killed but four that change nothing observable:
  - `<=` for `<` comparing two stages already known to differ;
  - `cut` treating a separator at index 0 as none (callers reject the empty part it leaves either way, twice);
  - dropping the chunk length from the program key, which only guards against chunk boundaries shifting with identical bytes.
- `go test ./...`, and `golangci-lint` for Windows and Linux, clean.

## Checklist

- [x] No personal paths, private map content, or credentials in the diff
- [x] `python plugin/skills/contribute/scripts/check_skills.py` reports 0 errors (the validator knows the new tool)

> **The `layout`, `zone` and `shape` ops this part adds are removed in part 9 (#79, 2e1db6c)**: map_edit now places brushes, patches and map text as the agent means them, and lays nothing out. The rest stays as described below.

Part 4 of the M1a stack (#52, a milestone of #51), split out of #68 so each PR's checks (coverage of changed lines, mutation) run on its own lines. Base: `feat/radiant-map-3-texturing` (#73). Merge bottom-up, each only with the owner's go-ahead; before merging a base with `--delete-branch`, retarget the PR above it to `main`, or GitHub closes it. Draft.

The agent edits the map open in the user's Radiant through the t7_radiant_bridge plugin (McReaper/t7_radiant_bridge#3).

## Seeing light, textures and models (2026-10-16)

- **`map_view` `bake`** runs Radiant's own bake (the lighting toolbar's bolt, at its L/M/H), waits for the console's `All Probes Done` and shoots under real lighting. Before it, an agent only ever saw fullbright and fake renders, so a sun leak or a dark room was invisible to it. Live on `zm_sonnet_blockout`: `All Probes Done (1.12 s)`, under 2 s for the call. The description says which render answers what: fullbright textures, fake shapes, bake light.
- **`map_materials` `show`** answers a sheet of the materials' color images, read from the install's TIFF and PNG textures, as Radiant's texture browser shows them. No Radiant needed, nothing added to the map, 272 + 393 tokens for six floors. The old board is now `board`, for seeing a material in the engine at its tile. The sheet also corrected a finding: the "black" wood Sonnet used is a light worn wood, which fullbright and the board had rendered black.
- **`map_models`** (new tool) finds xmodels by name words, the ones the install's maps place most first. `show` places 16 in Radiant, four to a row 128 units apart, shoots them from the front under fake lighting, and takes them back.
- **`hide` `sky`** hides the skybox's brushes, which drew over every shot from outside the map. The boards hide volumes and sky.
- **Framing:** `FrameBox` fits the box's corners instead of its bounding sphere, so flat boards and long rows fill the view. `View` also re-measures the lens on every framed shot and shoots again when it is more than 5% off. Correction to that commit's message: it blames a 1.7× too-far board on the lens guess, but after the change the labels didn't move. The guess was right, and the real cause was the model board's 3×3 layout of 256-unit cells. The re-measure stays as a safeguard, tested on the fake with a wider lens.
- **The room op** puts a `reflection_probe` in its middle, its radius reaching the corners (`"probe": false` for none). Its description says a hole's `at` is its middle, and a label that already starts with `t7kb: ` is marked once.
- **The skill's map-tools reference** gains which render answers what, `hide sky`, the sheet and the model board, a sun-leak section (probes, overlaps, all-`caulk_sun_shadow` brushes as Treyarch's `zm_giant_light.map` has them, then bake and look), and what replacing the template's start room leaves behind. It is at 1,983 of 2,000 words: the next addition splits it.

**Sun leaks on `zm_sonnet_blockout`:** fixed in Radiant through the map tools (probes in the kitchen, corridor and courtyard; two 8-unit `caulk_sun_shadow` caps over the closed rooms), baked, built (French linked). Waiting on the user's in-game check. A room op option for the cap waits on that result.

## A storey from a plan: the layout op (2026-10-16)

The user judged the room op too coarse for a real map: their `zm_test` (with its own house prefabs) is 4,312 brushes, 3,204 patches, 3,843 models, 427 prefabs and 295 lights around its rooms, so it would have been called once or twice. They proposed a layout tool, "start simple then we add more".

- **`map_edit`'s `layout` op** replaces `room`. The storey is a plan: named rooms, rectangles meeting along their edges, from wall centre to wall centre, with `openings` either `to` another room or on a `side`. A wall stands centred on every edge, and there is one wall where two rooms meet, where the room op doubled it. The walls along x take the corners and the walls along y stop against them, so no two pieces overlap and no corner is left open (tested on plans with a T, an L and a room set apart).
- **Materials:** each side of a wall takes the material of the room it looks into: `exterior` outside and in an `outdoor` room, a wall's end in a facade, and the top of a wall by the outside. Each room gets its floor, its ceiling (none when outdoor) and a probe. A door's threshold takes its room's floor. A window is an opening with a `sill`: 56 × 64 by default, Treyarch's scale standard. The answer's `part` names each piece (`hall floor`, `hall|kitchen wall`).
- **`map_check`:** a face is hidden when several brushes cover it together, not only one. A wall's end against two walls, or a floor's edge against a door's three pieces, now gets caulked and reported. On the stock prefabs, 30,425 faces are called hidden (was 27,912), 86% of them tool materials (was 85%).
- **Live, in a test Radiant on a copy of the template:** four rooms around a T-junction plus a courtyard, three doors, two windows and a door to the yard. It landed as one undo step in 0.8 s, all 48 pieces found back, `map_check` clean, one Undo taking it all back. The saved file's faces were as sent: the facade corner is brick, the end inside the kitchen is plaster. The shots came back blank, because the user's screen was asleep. The test Radiant was closed after; its ini was restored, and it left no dump and no change to the install.
- **`map_models`' `show` is now `board`**, as in `map_materials` (`show` there is the sheet made without Radiant). The map tools refuse an argument they don't take, naming the ones they do.
- **The skill** splits: `references/map-looks.md` holds materials, props, views and light, and `map-tools.md` keeps building and gains the layout section. Radiant's materia

CI speed. Measured on the run of #100 (job wall time): bench 81s, unit_test windows 1.23 62s, E2E windows 59s, E2E macOS 49s, CodeQL 46s, govulncheck 44s, the rest under 40s. The critical path is the paired himorime measurement, whose length is the measurement itself, so the suite is unchanged.

1. bench.yml runs on a pull request only when it changes Go code, go.mod/go.sum, internal/ (templates and fonts are embedded there), bench/, examples/ or the workflow. A documentation-only pull request cannot move a number, and no branch rule requires the check (the main ruleset only blocks deletion and force pushes).
2. Every pull request workflow that lacked it gets the concurrency group the gitleaks and mutation workflows use: a new push to the same pull request cancels the older run; push and schedule runs are never cancelled.

Checks kept: same workflows, jobs, OS and Go matrix on every code pull request and on main. Only documentation-only pull requests lose the benchmark.

candidates.body:
Rollout of the mutation rule recorded in the monorepo `AGENTS.md` ("Мутации: `--with-uncovered` обязателен"). No `src/` changes, so no release.

Testo credits a test only with the code its `#[Covers]` names, and Infection by default mutates only credited code. Code the tests execute but do not name therefore had no mutants and the gate reported `Not Covered: 0`. With `--with-uncovered` those mutants are generated and counted in the overall MSI.

## Changes

- `composer mutation`: `Composer\Config::disableProcessTimeout`, then `infection --threads=max --with-uncovered`.
- `infection.json5`: `PublicVisibility` off and `global-ignoreSourceCodeByRegex` for parameter defaults (as in the template). `minMsi` stays 95 with its existing comment.
- CHANGELOG entry. No new tests needed: every mutant is either killed or sits on a signature line.

## Numbers (local, pcov)

| | Before (`--with-uncovered`, old config) | After |
|---|---|---|
| Mutants | 28 | 26 counted |
| Not Covered | 2 | 0 |
| Escaped | 0 | 0 |
| Timed Out | 0 | 0 |
| Ignored | 0 | 2 (parameter defaults on signature lines) |
| Overall MSI | 92% | 100% (`minMsi` 95, unchanged) |

Without the ignore regex the two signature-line mutants stay Not Covered (no executable opcode under pcov) and the MSI is 26/28 = 92.9%, below 95. They are shown as `Ignored`, not hidden. `composer mutation` exits 0 twice in a row.

## What

- **Bridge to the engine's 0.9, the 1.0 candidate:** `rasuvaeff/understudy: ^0.8 || ^1.0` — the one union this package will carry, so there is no window in which `composer require` silently installs the 0.8 engine beside this adapter once the engine's 0.9 is out. This package itself stays on 0.x until Testo reaches 1.0 (`UnderstudyPlugin::configure()` is typed with Testo's `Internal\Container\Container`), so the follow-up minor drops the `^0.8` term.
- `infection/infection ^0.35`, the monorepo's single-major form.
- README ×2 and `llms.txt` stop dating engine behaviour («understudy 0.4+» beside `lean()`, «the engine from 0.3.0 refuses…»): with a floor of `^0.8` every engine this adapter installs beside behaves that way.

## Verification

`composer build` green (Unit 20 + Integration 6 tests), `composer rector` green.

Fixes #46

- The interceptor resolves strict stubs per test through `Rasuvaeff\Understudy\StrictStubs::resolve()`: method attribute > the case class running the test > its parents > the plugin's `strictStubs:` setting. Free-function tests keep the plugin setting. Without the attribute behaviour is unchanged.
- Requires `rasuvaeff/understudy` `^1.2` (the release that introduced the attribute).
- Tests: class on/off, method on/off, method over class, case class over declaring class, missing case reflection, function test, unchanged default (strict and lenient suite).
- README, README.ru, llms.txt, CHANGELOG `## 1.2.0 — 2026-11-21`.
- Local mutation (`--with-uncovered`, zend.assertions=-1): MSI 100% (38 killed, 2 ignored), gate 95.

## Summary by Sourcery

Support per-test and per-class strict-stub configuration through `#[StrictStubs]` while retaining the plugin setting as the default.

New Features:
- Honor `#[StrictStubs]` attributes on test classes and methods when determining strict-stub verification behavior, with method-level settings taking precedence over class-level settings and class settings taking precedence over the suite default.

Enhancements:
- Preserve suite-level strict-stub behavior for tests without attributes and free-function tests.
- Use the running test case class when resolving inherited test methods.

Build:
- Raise the required `rasuvaeff/understudy` dependency to `^1.2`.

Documentation:
- Document strict-stub attribute overrides and update dependency requirements in the English and Russian README files and changelog.

Tests:
- Add coverage for class-level, method-level, inherited-class, fallback, function-test, and unchanged suite-level strict-stub behavior.

## Summary

- A plain test that starts while the understudy context already holds doubles now fails **before its body runs**, with a message naming the cause and the fix — the counterpart of the `#[Before]` guard in `understudy-phpunit`. The message is adapted to Testo (data provider / `#[BeforeClass]` instead of `setUpBeforeClass()` / `setUp()`). The reset in `finally` still runs, so the next test starts clean.
- Reproduced first with a real runner (new `OutsideTest` fixture): before the change an array data provider's doubles were silently verified by dataset #0 and dataset #1 hit a bare `ForgottenDouble`; a generator provider passed by accident. Now both are refused; `#[BeforeClass]` doubles too. `#[BeforeTest]` doubles are unaffected (the lifecycle interceptor is innermost). Doubles built in the case constructor are **not** caught: Testo constructs the case inside the test's pipeline — documented, not claimed.
- Scope matches verification: inline tests and benchmarks are not refused, only reset.
- Docs: README.md + README.ru.md (lifecycle list), llms.txt, AGENTS.md (lifecycle contract, pipeline-position note).
- CHANGELOG: `## 1.1.0 — 2026-11-20`, with a note that a suite passing by accident turns red.

#46 (per-class/method `strictStubs`) is left open: the approved proposal is one attribute shared by both bridges, which has to live in the engine first — filed as rasuvaeff/understudy#185.

Local: `composer build` green, `composer rector` clean, mutation (`--with-uncovered`, `zend.assertions=-1`) 33/33 killed, 2 ignored, MSI 100% (minMsi 95).

Fixes #47

## Summary by Sourcery

Refuse plain tests that start with doubles created outside their own lifecycle and reset the context safely afterward.

New Features:
- Reject plain tests that begin with doubles left in the context by data providers or `#[BeforeClass]` hooks, with guidance for creating them within the test lifecycle.

Bug Fixes:
- Prevent leaked external doubles from being silently verified by the wrong test and producing misleading subsequent failures.

Enhancements:
- Preserve reset behavior after refused tests and limit the new guard to plain tests while leaving inline tests and benchmarks unaffected.
- Document lifecycle guard behavior and pipeline-position boundaries in English and Russian project documentation.

Documentation:
- Document the filled-context guard, supported lifecycle placement, and remediation guidance in the project documentation.

Tests:
- Add unit and integration coverage for array and generator providers, `#[BeforeClass]`, `#[BeforeTest]`, reset behavior, and non-plain test types.

Chores:
- Release version 1.1.0 with the filled-context behavior change recorded in the changelog.

Cuts 0.3.0 from what #24 merged, and moves the engine constraint to `rasuvaeff/understudy` `^0.8` — **as a single term**.

A minor rather than a patch: a test that creates no double is no longer touched at all, so its assertion count and a `Risky` verdict of the runner's both change back to what they would be without this adapter. That is the fix, and it is observable in any suite that has such tests — which is every suite.

The accumulating `^0.5 || ^0.6 || ^0.7` is gone. It had to be widened by hand on every core release, and a package that misses one becomes uninstallable beside its own engine.

Green against core v0.8.0 from Packagist: `composer build` including the integration suite (real Testo processes), mutation MSI 100% at the 95 gate.

candidates.body:
The `note`-level findings of the 2026-09-03 audit for this package.

| Note | Fix |
|---|---|
| the "benchmark: reset without verify" claim is pinned by nothing | a test over every non-plain `TestType`, verified in both directions |
| `examples/` is in no gate, and its `assert()` calls vanish under `zend.assertions=-1` | `@examples` in `composer build`, checks that throw |
| the `Seams` provider is not named `<method>Provider` | renamed |
| some fixtures carry `@internal`, some do not | all of them do |

## The benchmark fixture that is not here

A real `#[Bench]` fixture was the obvious way to pin the claim, and it does not work: the benchmark aborts in Testo's own runner (`PipelineFailure`) with **no understudy code in the body at all**. Pinning the claim that way would have measured the runner, not this adapter.

`$info->identity->type` is where `runTest()` reads the decision, so the test drives it there — with every `TestType` that is not `Test`, so a type added to the enum lands in the provider on its own. Dropping the type check from the interceptor reddens all three datasets; the reset half is checked by a plain test that follows and must start idle.

## Verification

- `composer build` green, examples included.
- `composer mutation` on the PHP 8.4 image: 24 of 24 killed, MSI 100%, gate 95.

No release is needed for any of this — it is tests, an example gate and docblocks.

candidates.body:
Fixes #21. Fixes #22. Fixes #23.

## #21

Testo marks a passing test `risky` when it recorded no assertion. `UnderstudyInterceptor` takes that verdict back when its own record is the only one in the history — deliberately narrow, and documented as such. But `verify()` ran for **every** completed test, always recorded a success and always added an assertion, so the condition held for a test understudy had never touched:

```
### with the plugin                 ### without the plugin
 ✓ emptyBodyNoDoublesAtAll           ? emptyBodyNoDoublesAtAll
 ✓ bodyWithoutAssertionsOrDoubles    ? bodyWithoutAssertionsOrDoubles
 2 tests · 2 assertions              2 tests · 0 assertions
 2 passed                            2 risky
```

Installing the adapter for one clear place of verification silently cost the project a runner check across the whole suite, including tests written before the adapter existed.

A test that created no double is now left alone entirely — `Understudy::idle()` decides, before anything is recorded. Nothing is added to its assertion count and its `Risky` verdict stands.

The four fixture suites in `tests/Integration` each drop exactly one assertion, and each of those is the body that holds no double — which is the change, measured through a real runner process rather than asserted about.

## #22

Both READMEs pointed at `Understudy::strict($double)` as the per-double form of strict stubs. It is strict **dispatch** — "fail on any call no expectation matched" — and has nothing to say about a stub that was configured and never called: verified by running it, the test passes. The per-double equivalent is `when(…)->times(n)`, which fails as it should.

## #23

Verification runs **after** your teardown here (interceptor, outside `#[AfterTest]`) and **before** it under `understudy-phpunit` (`assertPostConditions()` precedes `tearDown()`), while both READMEs promise "the same, through a trait" and document the order only for `reset()`. A test whose expectation is fulfilled by teardown itself passes in one runner and fails in the other. Both READMEs and `llms.txt` now say so; the same sentence goes into the PHPUnit adapter.

`llms.txt` also gains the note that `UnderstudyInterceptor` takes the same `strictStubs` argument as `UnderstudyPlugin`.

## Verification

`composer build` green, integration suite included. `make mutation`: Covered Code MSI **100%** against the `minMsi = 95` gate.

## Summary

Independent investor-perspective review of AIPEA v1.3.2, with five actionable follow-ups tracked on the roadmap.

- **New:** `docs/claude/audits/investor-review-2026-04-11.md` — 9-criterion scorecard (39/45 = 87%), verdict, and five detailed recommendations.
- **Updated:** `docs/ROADMAP.md` — adds a new **P5: Investor Review Follow-ups** section (P5a–P5e) mirroring the recommendations so the work is tracked alongside the existing P1–P4 backlog.

## Scorecard Highlights

| Criterion | Score |
|---|---:|
| Product judgment | 4 / 5 |
| Architectural soundness | **5 / 5** |
| Technical depth | 4 / 5 |
| Code craftsmanship | 4 / 5 |
| Test discipline | **5 / 5** |
| Engineering process | **5 / 5** |
| Honesty & self-awareness | **5 / 5** |
| Shipping velocity | 4 / 5 |
| Risk profile | 3 / 5 |
| **Total** | **39 / 45 (87%)** |

Strongest signals: the dependency graph in `CLAUDE.md §4` is enforced in code (not aspirational); `mypy --strict` passes with only 2 documented `# type: ignore` lines across 9.6K LOC; the bug-hunt wave methodology in `KNOWN_ISSUES.md` is genuinely closed-loop (Wave 18 resolves deferred bugs from prior waves with citations).

Weakest signals: bus-factor 1 (every commit from a single human), FedRAMP is labeled honestly as a stub but claimed prominently enough to be a commercial liability, and broad `except Exception:` blocks in `src/aipea/cli.py` (lines 191, 220, 283, 391, 438) and `src/aipea/config.py:444` prevent consumers from discriminating failure modes.

## The Five Recommendations (now P5a–P5e)

1. **P5a — Second-reviewer coverage on security-critical modules.** Contract a part-time senior reviewer (~4 hrs/week); add `CODEOWNERS` requiring their review on `src/aipea/security.py`, `src/aipea/__init__.py`, and `pyproject.toml`. Highest leverage: simultaneously removes the top investor objection *and* hardens the most sensitive module.
2. **P5b — Resolve FedRAMP: ship it or stop claiming it.** Decision fork between finding a design-partner customer (Path A, months) or removing the claim with an ADR (Path B, one afternoon). Current state is the worst of both worlds.
3. **P5c — Custom exception hierarchy + tightened CLI error handling.** Create `src/aipea/errors.py` with five domain-specific subclasses; walk each broad `except Exception:` block and convert it. Fits the existing bug-hunt methodology as **Wave 19**. 1–2 days.
4. **P5d — Promote mutation testing to gating + performance regression suite.** Move `mutmut` from nightly `continue-on-error` into a dedicated CI job with a ratcheting floor; add `benchmarks/` `pytest-benchmark` suite with a 20% p95 regression threshold per tier. ~1 week.
5. **P5e — Build a commercial validation surface.** Non-engineering: case studies, metrics page, GitHub Discussions, design-partner outreach. The codebase can't do BD work, but BD outcomes constrain which technical items (P5b Path A, P3b) are worth building.

## If Only One Item Ships

**P5a (second reviewer)** — highest leverage by far. Everything else can wait a quarter; that one can't.

## Test Plan

- [ ] No code changes; this PR is documentation-only
- [ ] Verify `docs/claude/audits/investor-review-2026-04-11.md` renders on GitHub
- [ ] Verify the new **P5** section in `docs/ROADMAP.md` renders and cross-links to the audit file
- [ ] Confirm `docs/ROADMAP.md` footer date updated to `2026-04-11`

candidates.body:
## Summary

Wave C1 of the 2026-04-11 consolidated investor-review response plan. Installs an **automated dual-AI second-reviewer gate** (\`gpt-5.4-pro\` + Codex CLI via \`openai/codex-action@v1\`) that fires on every PR touching AIPEA's security-critical paths. Closes the bus-factor-1 finding from both investor reviews (positive §P5a and adversarial §5.1).

Follows undercurrentai/AIPEA#20 (Wave A), #21 (Wave B), #22 (Wave C2), #23 (Wave C3).

## Why this design

**The first-draft workflow was materially wrong in five places.** A Context7 + Exa research pass against the OpenAI docs caught all five before any code was committed:

| First draft | Reality (verified) |
|---|---|
| Model ID formatted as "GPT 5.4 Pro" | \`gpt-5.4-pro\` (lowercase, hyphenated) |
| Tried Chat Completions first | **Responses API only** per the model card |
| Synchronous call with 10min timeout | **Background mode + polling required** — model card explicitly says "may take several minutes; use background mode to avoid timeouts" |
| \`npm install -g @openai/codex\` + custom Python wrapper | **Use the official \`openai/codex-action@v1\`** which installs the CLI, starts a Responses-API proxy, and runs \`codex exec\` under a sandbox strategy |
| Missing \`reasoning.effort\` | Required for reasoning models; set to \`high\` for this gate |

Research sources (recorded in the plan file under Wave C1 → Research sources):
- OpenAI Python SDK (\`/openai/openai-python\`, v2.11.0 on Context7)
- Reasoning models guide (\`platform.openai.com/docs/guides/reasoning?api-mode=responses\`)
- \`gpt-5.4-pro\` model card (\`platform.openai.com/docs/models/gpt-5.4-pro\`)
- Codex GitHub Action (\`/openai/codex-action\` + \`developers.openai.com/codex/github-action/\`)
- Codex CLI reference (\`developers.openai.com/codex/cli/reference/\`)
- \`actions/github-script\` (\`/actions/github-script\`) — confirmed \`require()\` IS exposed in its sandbox (the PostToolUse hook flagging this was wrong)

## Files

| File | Status | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| \`.github/CODEOWNERS\` | modified | Add \`@joshuakirby\` as the accountable human reviewer on security-critical paths. Preserves existing \`@ThermoclineLeviathan\` entries. |
| \`.github/workflows/ai-second-review.yml\` | **NEW** | Two parallel jobs (\`gpt-review\`, \`codex-review\`) on \`pull_request\` with the gated \`paths:\` filter. 30min timeout per job. Concurrency group per PR with cancel-in-progress. |
| \`.github/scripts/gpt_review.py\` | **NEW** (~301 LOC) | Python script invoking \`gpt-5.4-pro\` via Responses API in background mode. Polls until terminal state with a 25-minute cap. System prompt embeds AIPEA-specific review mandates. Structured fallback Markdown on any failure. |
| \`.github/codex/prompts/second-review.md\` | **NEW** | Markdown prompt file passed to \`openai/codex-action\` via \`prompt-file\`. Same review mandate as the GPT job but with Codex-specific shell-verification instructions. |

## Gated paths (\`paths:\` filter)

\`\`\`
src/aipea/security.py
src/aipea/__init__.py
src/aipea/errors.py
pyproject.toml
.github/workflows/**
.github/CODEOWNERS
\`\`\`

Matches the \`CODEOWNERS\` security-critical set. Deliberately narrow — widening to all \`src/aipea/**\` is a one-line change if we decide the added signal is worth the added cost.

## Workflow structure

### \`gpt-review\` job (30min timeout)

1. Checkout PR head at \`fetch-depth: 0\` (need history for diff)
2. \`git fetch\` base ref + \`git diff origin/\${base}...HEAD -- \${GATED_PATHS} > pr_diff.patch\`
3. Truncate diff at 200 KB with a visible marker (budget guardrail)
4. \`pip install openai>=2.11\`
5. Run \`gpt_review.py --diff pr_diff.patch --output gpt_review.md\`
6. Load review Markdown into \`\$GITHUB_ENV\` as a multiline variable named \`REVIEW_BODY\`
7. \`actions/github-script\` reads \`process.env.REVIEW_BODY\`, finds/updates the comment carrying marker \`<!-- ai-second-review:gpt -->\`, posts/edits it
8. Append review to \`\$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY\` for audit trail

### \`codex-review\` job (30min timeout)

1. Same checkout + diff preparation (shared \`GATED_PATHS\` env var keeps the list in sync between jobs)
2. \`openai/codex-action@v1\` with:
   \`\`\`yaml
   openai-api-key: \${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}
   prompt-file: .github/codex/prompts/second-review.md
   output-file: codex_review.md
   model: gpt-5.4-pro

Implements the 1.0.0 roadmap: M1 (foundation), M2 (receiving), M3 (sending), M4 (moderation and display).

Related: #2, #6 · Resolves: #3, #4, #5

## M1 – Foundation (TYPO3 13 + 14)
- TYPO3 `^13.4 || ^14.0`, PHP `^8.2`; `extra.typo3/cms.version` + `providesPackages` for TYPO3 14.3
- PECL `ext-xmlrpc` replaced by our own `XmlRpcCodec` (no DOCTYPE, no external entities)
- Site set `webicorns/pongback` as the only integration path: TypoScript, `route-enhancers.yaml` (native in v14, via listener in v13), site settings
- No `ext_tables.sql`: tables and columns come from TCA; columns for hidden/starttime/endtime/language come from `ctrl`
- Sites without the set get no Pingback features

## M2 – Receiving
- Our own middleware before TypoScript rendering, all fault codes of the specification, rate limit per IP
- Protocol neutral core `Classes/Mention` (basis for a future Webmention endpoint)
- SSRF protection: public http(s) hosts on default ports only, every redirect checked, IP pinning, timeout, 1 MiB
- Plain text only, moderation by default, `BeforePingbackCreateEvent`

## M3 – Sending
- DataHandler hook queues one message per changed page and language (workspace changes on publish)
- Messenger handler: renders the page, takes the links of `<main>`/`<article>`/`<body>` (max. 50), endpoint discovery, `pingback.ping`, retries after 5 min / 1 h
- Log table `tx_pongback_sent`, each Pingback only once per page and link
- `PingbackQueue` sets the transport explicitly: TYPO3 13 would otherwise also send synchronously via the `*` route
- EXT:webhooks removed

## M4 – Moderation and display
- Module **Web > Pongback**: Pingbacks of the page tree, approve/hide/delete via POST + token, through the DataHandler (permissions, history, caches)
- Email notification (`AfterPingbackCreatedEvent`) with a link into the module via the login redirect
- Plugins cached with the page (cache tag of the table), correct page ID, language, pagination; "Latest" limited to the current site
- Dashboard widget: newest first, linking website, its own button and group, respects page permissions
- Removed: old modules, AJAX via GET, pagination traits, own cache + DataMap hook, Page TSconfig (wizard, list module, dashboard templates)

## Bugs found by the tests (fixed)
- v13: DI container failed while the extension configuration was not written yet
- Hidden pages were accepted as Pingback targets; `https://user@host` was not rejected; the excerpt cut off the end of the text
- v13: messages were also handled synchronously while saving in the backend
- Sites without the set announced the endpoint and accepted/sent Pingbacks
- Email subject and plain text part were HTML escaped

## Tests and QA
- 245 unit and 52 functional tests (SQLite), green locally against TYPO3 13.4.40 and 14.3.12 and in CI (PHP 8.2–8.4)
- Including: rendering of the module and the dashboard widget, frontend plugins via real frontend requests, DataHandler permissions (admin vs. editor)
- Infection: covered MSI 91 % (CI fails below 90 %); PHPStan v13/v14 without errors; php-cs-fixer, Rector, docs rendering in CI
- Not automated: real network requests to external sites (stubbed), click-through in a real backend

## Open (#6, by the maintainer)
- Decide the version number and set it with `tailor set-version`, tag → TER (automatic)

candidates.body:
Adds [Webmention](https://www.w3.org/TR/webmention/) (W3C recommendation) alongside Pingback, makes sending problems visible and prepares release 0.10.0 (beta).

Related: #6 (planned there as "1.1: Webmention support")

## Receiving Webmentions
- Endpoint `https://<site>/webmention` (page type `1709405325111`, route via the site set; via the listener in v13)
- Discovery: `Link: <…>; rel="webmention"` header and `<link rel="webmention">`, using the existing discovery settings
- `WebmentionEndpoint` only does quick checks (http(s) URLs, different, target is a visible page of the site, rate limit) and answers **202 Accepted**; 400 for invalid requests, 429 when rate limited
- The worker verifies the source: `MentionReceiver::synchronize()` **creates** (moderation, events, email as for Pingbacks), **updates** title/excerpt of a known mention, **removes** it when the source is gone (404/410) or no longer links; temporary problems are retried after 5 min / 1 h
- Site setting `pongback.receive.webmention` (default on)

## Sending Webmentions
- Discovery prefers Webmention: `Link` header, then the first `<link>`/`<a rel="webmention">` in document order (empty `href` = the page itself, query string kept); otherwise Pingback
- `WebmentionClient`: form POST, 2xx = sent, 4xx final (except 429), 429/5xx/network retried
- Webmentions are sent again on every page change (so receivers update); Pingbacks still once; retries only repeat what failed
- **Removed links** get one more Webmention (the receiver removes the mention), then the log entry is deleted
- Setting `pongback.send.webmention` (default on)

## Sending problems
- The module Web > Pongback lists rejected and failed sends of the page tree (protocol, answer of the linked site, attempts); the dashboard widget counts them; both respect page permissions
- New event `SendingFailedEvent` when linked pages could not be notified for good (newly rejected, or failed after the last attempt); `NotifyEditors` sends one email per page to `pongback.notification.emailTo`

## Fixes
- **Routing of the messages is respected**: `ext_localconf.php` overwrote any routing from `config/system/additional.php` with `doctrine`, so the documented routing never worked. Found by a new functional test for the setup without a worker
- A linked page answering 404/410 is no longer retried (new rejection reason `SourceGone`, Pingback still answers fault 16)

## Other
- `PingbackQueue` → `Messaging\MessageQueue`; middleware `pingback-discovery` → `discovery`
- Module, dashboard widget and email show the protocol
- Docs: new chapter "Webmention"; "Run the worker" explains cron (user, paths, overlapping runs), scheduler, process managers, how to check it, and the setup without a worker (synchronous routing and its costs); PlantUML sequence diagrams for receiving a Pingback, receiving a Webmention and sending
- Version **0.10.0 (beta)** in composer.json, ext_emconf.php, guides.xml, README and changelog

## Tests
- 355 unit and 66 functional tests, green locally against TYPO3 13.4.40 and 14.3.12 and in CI (PHP 8.2–8.4)
- Discovery cases modelled on the spec rules (as tested by webmention.rocks); `/webmention` through the real frontend; module and widget rendering with sending problems; emails incl. plain text; synchronous routing without a worker
- Infection: covered MSI 92 %; PHPStan v13/v14 without errors; php-cs-fixer, Rector and docs rendering green in CI
- Not automated: a real exchange with webmention.rocks / external sites (network stubbed); the diagrams render without warnings in CI, but I could not view the images

## After merging
`git tag -a 0.10.0 -m "Webmention: receive and send" && git push origin 0.10.0` publishes to TER (Packagist updates automatically).

Bumps [io.jsonwebtoken:jjwt](https://github.com/jwtk/jjwt) from 0.9.1 to 0.13.0.
Release notes

Sourced from io.jsonwebtoken:jjwt's releases.

0.13.0

This is the last minor JJWT release branch that will support Java 7.

Any necessary emergency bug fixes will be fixed in subsequent 0.13.x patch releases, but all new development, including Java 8 compatible changes, will be in the next minor (0.14.0) release.

All future JJWT major and minor versions ( 0.14.0 and later) will require Java 8 or later.

What's Changed

This release contains a single change:

  • The previously private JacksonDeserializer(ObjectMapper objectMapper, Map<String, Class<?>> claimTypeMap) constructor is now public for those that want register a claims type converter on their own specified ObjectMapper instance. Thank you to @​kesrishubham2510 for PR #972. See Issue 914.

Full Changelog: https://github.com/jwtk/jjwt/compare/0.12.7...0.13.0

0.12.7

This patch release:

  • Adds a new Maven BOM! This is useful for multi-module projects. See Issue 967.

  • Allows the JwtParserBuilder to have empty nested algorithm collections, effectively disabling the parser's associated feature:

    • Emptying the zip() nested collection disables JWT decompression.
    • Emptying the sig() nested collection disables JWS mac/signature verification (i.e. all JWSs will be unsupported/rejected).
    • Emptying either the enc() or key() nested collections disables JWE decryption (i.e. all JWEs will be unsupported/rejected)

    See Issue 996.

  • Fixes bug 961 where JwtParserBuilder nested collection builders were not correctly replacing algorithms with the same id.

  • Ensures a JwkSet's keys collection is no longer entirely secret/redacted by default. This was an overzealous default that was unnecessarily restrictive; the keys collection itself should always be public, and each individual key within should determine which fields should be redacted when printed. See Issue 976.

  • Improves performance slightly by ensuring all jjwt-api utility methods that create *Builder instances (Jwts.builder(), Jwts.parserBuilder(), Jwks.builder(), etc) no longer use reflection.

    Instead,static factories are created via reflection only once during initial jjwt-api classloading, and then *Builders are created via standard instantiation using the new operator thereafter. This also benefits certain environments that may not have ideal ClassLoader implementations (e.g. Tomcat in some cases).

    NOTE: because this changes which classes are loaded via reflection, any environments that must explicitly reference reflective class names (e.g. GraalVM applications) will need to be updated to reflect the new factory class names.

    See Issue 988.

  • Upgrades the Gson dependency to 2.11.0

  • Upgrades the BouncyCastle dependency to 1.78.1

New Contributors

  • @​sigpwned made their first contribution in jwtk/jjwt#968
  • @​TheMrMilchmann made their first contribution in jwtk/jjwt#979

candidates.body:
The nightly cargo-mutants job ran out of its 75 minutes every night since
2026-11-19 without a surviving mutant: a day's diff held 236 to 3,120 mutants
and the unmutated test run had grown to 355 s.

.cargo/mutants.toml builds the dependencies at opt-level 3 and without debug
info for every cargo-mutants run. Every agent-guard test binary run on its
own went from 207 s to 58 s (8 cores); the time was in unoptimised regex,
YAML and tree-sitter code, not in the tests. No test suite is left out. A
minimum test timeout of 300 s keeps a slow survivor from reading as a hang.

The nightly is now a plan job that counts the day's mutants and splits them
into up to twenty shards of about forty, the shards, and a summary job that
says "tested X of Y". A shard whose budget runs out passes with a warning when
nothing it tested survived; a survivor, a hang, a diff that does not apply, a
missing memory cap or a cargo-mutants error still fail it.
scripts/mutants-diff-verdict.sh holds that decision. A manual run can diff
against a chosen commit (diff_base).


Proof run on this branch, the last 26 hours of main as the diff: https://github.com/InnerWarden/inner-warden/actions/runs/45959806415

- The plan job split 2,836 mutants into 20 shards of 142. The unmutated test run took 95 s (355 s before).
- The shards tested 369 of 2,836 before their budget ran out (about a dozen per night before). Each mutant costs about 12 minutes: a rebuild of 440 to 556 s, which relinks every test binary, plus about 240 s of tests.
- 85 of the 369 survived, in code changed that day. Each shard is red on its own survivors and says so in the summary ("tested X of Y, N survived"), not on its budget.

candidates.body:
## What

The weekly mutation sweep of the screening engine (`threats.rs`, `shell.rs`, `session.rs`) has ended red every Sunday since 2026-10-18: the list grew from 2,540 to about 4,400 mutants and twenty shards no longer fit their budget. Given forty shards, thirteen of them were then killed by a mutant that allocated without end and left no report. This makes the sweep finish, makes its result mean something, and starts burning down what it found.

## The sweep

- **Forty shards**, each with a per-mutant timeout of three times the unmutated suite instead of a fixed 120 s, and a budget of 180 minutes per shard.
- **A memory cap on every test binary** (`scripts/mutants-test-runner.sh`, a cargo target runner with `ulimit -v`). A mutant that allocates without end now fails its own test run and is counted as caught, instead of taking the runner down. The job fails if the tests ran and no binary ran under the cap.
- **Wall-clock ceilings off during a sweep** (`IW_NO_WALL_CLOCK_CEILINGS=1`, honoured by `tests/hot_path_budget.rs`, `tests/guard_check_cost.rs` and `tests/guard_lowering_parse.rs`). In two sweeps of the same 4,372 mutants a time ceiling was the only test that failed for 139 mutants in one run and for 92 others in the next: a busy runner decided what a sweep saw, and a ceiling is not a test of the mutated line. The sweep of the merged tree showed it a third time: the ceiling 1.6.12 added in `tests/guard_lowering_parse.rs` was the only test that failed for 76 mutants, at 3.0 to 4.9 s against 3 s. Run again with the ceiling off, 68 of them survive, 1 times out and 7 are caught by a test. Outside a sweep every ceiling holds.
- **A baseline of known survivors** (`crates/agent-guard/mutants-baseline.txt`, checked by `scripts/mutants-baseline-check.sh`). A shard fails only on a survivor that is not listed. Keys are `file / function / mutation`, without line and column, so an edit above a survivor does not turn it into a new one; a key may appear in a run no more often than in the list. Each line says why it is there: not killed yet (with the sweep date), or equivalent (with the reason).
- The check exits 2, and the shard fails, when the sweep left no report to compare: a check that compared nothing is not a pass.
- The nightly job over changed lines does not read the baseline: code changed today must have no survivor at all.

## Tests

139 tests in `crates/agent-guard/src/mutant_kills/` (16 files, one per reader the sweep found weak), each written against a named surviving mutant and each asserting behaviour of the public screen, not only the internal.

## Production code

- `shell.rs`: `node_expands_tainted_variable` drops its check for a quoted heredoc body. tree-sitter-bash scans such a body raw, so it holds no expansion node and the check could never decide anything (pinned by `a_quoted_heredoc_body_has_no_expansion_nodes`). Were that ever untrue, the removal can only flag more, never less.
- `threats.rs`: the word walk of the guard-lowering reader names the slice of words after the current one once (`rest`) instead of spelling it out in each arm. No behaviour change.

## Merge of main (guard 1.6.12)

1.6.12 rewrote several readers these tests were written against. The tests follow main: where main changed a behaviour on purpose (ssh, scp and sftp take no long option, so `--identity` is no longer excused as key use) the test asserts main's behaviour; one test whose target is gone (the word limit of a brace expansion, now a byte limit that main tests) is removed.

The sweep was run again on the merged tree (run 43020449252): 5,223 mutants, every one of the forty shards finished, in 75 to 142 minutes. The baseline is regenerated from that run and from the re-run of the 76 above, not appended to: 1,200 survivors (1,034 missed, 166 timeouts) against 3,915 caught and 108 unviable. A line keeps its date and its reason when the earlier list held the same key; an `equivalent:` reason written for a function that 1.6.12 rewrote is dropped, because it describes code that is gone.

## Checked

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean.
- `cargo test -p innerwarden-agent-guard`: 1,216 passed, 0 failed (Linux x86_64).
- `tests/hot_path_budget.rs` and `tests/guard_lowering_parse.rs` pass with and without `IW_NO_WALL_CLOCK_CEILINGS`.
- Each of the forty shard reports of run 43020449252 passes `scripts/mutants-baseline-check.sh` against the regenerated list, and so does the report of the re-run.
- The lines this PR changes in production code hold 8 mutants, all caught.

## Not in this PR

- The sweep still names three files. The files 1.6.12 added beside them (about 1,800 mutants) are not in it: they need more shards and a list of their own.
- The nightly job over changed lines cannot finish a day the size of a release. The day 1.6.12 landed holds 3,221 mutants against a budget of 75 minutes; 82 ran. That job is red in run 43020449252 for that reason, and it will be red on main the night after 1.6.12 with or without this PR.

candidates.body:
The nightly has not completed once since 2026-08-06. **Fourteen runs**: cancelled through the 12th, failed from the 13th, and not one uploaded a report.

## It is arithmetic, not a flake

Measured on this tree:

| | |
|---|---|
| mutants over the three screened files | **2,540** |
| rate on the CI runner | 0.93 / minute |
| work implied | **~45 hours** |
| job budget | 2.8 hours |

Sixteen times more work than time. And with `--no-shuffle` the order is deterministic, so every night retested the same first ~112 mutants — **4.4%** — and died there. The other 95.6% of the screening engine had never been mutation-tested at all.

## A second defect underneath it

The step ended in

```
|| echo "::warning::cargo-mutants did not finish inside 150m"
```

which collapses every non-zero exit into a warning. cargo-mutants exits **2 when mutants survive**, which is the entire point of the check — so a surviving mutant could never fail this job, even on the 4.4% it did reach.

## Split by what each question is worth

- **nightly** — `--in-diff` over the last day. A heavy day on this crate measured **56 mutants, about an hour**, inside a 75m budget. It answers *"do the tests check what we just wrote?"*, which has a short feedback loop and someone to act on it.
- **weekly** — the full sweep, 20 shards, Sunday. 127 mutants each, ~135 minutes.

Exit codes are read rather than swallowed: `0` clean, `2` a mutant survived (**fails**), `3` cargo-mutants timed out, `5`/`6` the diff no longer applies so the check did *not* run, `124` the outer budget was not enough. Each says what it means and what to do about it.

## The shard matrix is zero-indexed, and that is not cosmetic

`--shard k/n` takes k in `0..n-1`, so the obvious `1..20` matrix drops shard 0 and spends a job on an empty shard 20. Verified by listing every shard:

```
shard  0/20 -> 127        shard 20/20 -> 0
shard  1/20 -> 127        sum over 0..19 -> 2540  (the full list)
shard 19/20 -> 127
```

A sweep that looks complete while quietly skipping 5% of itself is the exact failure this workflow exists to prevent.

## Also

Concurrency is keyed by schedule so the Sunday sweep and a nightly cannot cancel each other, and a manual run does the cheap job only unless the full-sweep box is ticked — twenty jobs by accident is a poor reward for clicking "Run workflow".

Everything above was verified locally against cargo-mutants 25.3.1, the same major the workflow installs: counts, shard arithmetic, the empty-diff case and the in-diff size are measured, not estimated.

## Worth noting

This rework came out of reading the report the broken job *did* manage to emit. Its surviving mutants pointed at an untested function, and following that lead found a live `rm -rf /` bypass, fixed in #86. The sweep earned its keep while broken.

candidates.body:
## What was broken

The nightly `miri` job had **no time budget**. It ran to GitHub's 6-hour platform cap and was killed. Every scheduled run from **2026-08-06 to 2026-08-12** ended that way, and the run reported **"cancelled"** — which reads as harmless.

So nothing was checked for undefined behaviour for a week, and nothing said so. The workflow's own header says the point is that *"a failure is SEEN, on a schedule"*.

The log shows exactly where it stopped:

```
05:01:33  running 27 tests
05:01:34  test prune_tests::a_pruned_session_never_reuses_a_command_id ... ok
05:01:34  test prune_tests::a_small_graph_is_untouched ... ok
11:01:02  ##[error]The operation was canceled.
```

Two tests in one second, then six hours on the next.

## Why

Miri interprets every operation. Three tests here build `MAX_NODES`-scale graphs — 20k nodes, one of them with 700-byte labels to reach ~14 MB — because that is what it takes to prove a **byte** budget rather than a node count. Under an interpreter that does not finish.

They are now `#[cfg_attr(miri, ignore)]`. Nothing is lost: neither `graph` nor `notify` contains a single `unsafe` block, and the remaining tests exercise the same paths.

## The part worth reading

**Skipping the two obvious offenders was not enough.** The run simply hung on a third, `edges_that_would_dangle_are_removed_with_their_node`, and that only surfaced because I installed miri and ran it rather than assuming the fix worked.

So this adds a check that fails when a cap-scale test is added without the skip, instead of trusting the next author to remember. Its first version had a false positive — it read past a test's closing brace into the next one's doc comment, which mentions `MAX_NODES` in prose. It now cuts at the brace and ignores comments.

```
these tests build MAX_NODES-scale graphs but are not skipped under miri, so the
nightly undefined-behaviour job will hang until the 6-hour platform cap kills it
and report only "cancelled": edges_that_would_dangle_are_removed_with_their_node
```

## Verified, not assumed

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `miri test -p innerwarden-graph` | never finished (6 h, killed) | **220 s** — 25 passed, 3 ignored |
| `miri test -p innerwarden-notify` | never reached | **7 s** — 41 passed |

**No undefined behaviour anywhere.** The code was fine; we just could not see it.

## Also

candidates.body:
Found by chasing a surviving mutant, not by review.

The nightly mutation sweep has reported the same MISSED mutants in `substitution_bodies` for two weeks — the depth counter and the bounds. Every one survives, which says the tests never exercise nesting or edges. Neutering the counter by hand confirms it: **409 tests pass** with the increment replaced by a no-op.

Probing that function led somewhere worse than the untested branch.

## The bypass

Measured against the shipped guard, the shapes of a root wipe it recognises:

| command | recognised |
|---|---|
| `rm -rf /` | yes |
| `sudo rm -rf /` | yes |
| `FOO=1 rm -rf /` | yes |
| `"" rm -rf /` | yes |
| `'' rm -rf /` | yes |
| `$() rm -rf /` | **no** |
| `$(true) rm -rf /` | **no** |
| `` `` rm -rf / `` | **no** |

All three of the last group delete the filesystem. A command substitution in command position expands to its output, and when that output is empty the next token becomes the command.

## Why

`rm_command_index` walks a prefix of env assignments and wrappers (`sudo`, `env`, `timeout`, `nice`, …) and returns `None` on anything else. The tokenizer discards the parentheses, so `$(true) rm -rf /` arrives as `["$", "true", "rm", "-rf", "/"]`, the walk hits `$`, and the whole segment is dismissed.

Empty quotes were fine only because the tokenizer drops them entirely — which is why the gap was not obvious from reading the code.

## The change

Leading substitutions are removed from the segment before tokenizing, with nesting counted so the whole prefix goes.

**Only leading ones**, and that restriction is the safety argument:

- stripping them everywhere would erase `rm -rf $(echo /)`, where the substitution is the *target* rather than a prefix, and that shape is recognised today;
- nothing inside a substitution is lost either, because `destructive_rm_root` already feeds every substitution body through this same check — inner and outer text are each judged as the shell would run them;
- an unbalanced substitution is left alone rather than guessed at, since consuming to the end of the string would swallow the command it was hiding.

## Tests

Six. The bypass test **fails with the fix removed** (verified). The other five pin what must not move: the shapes that already worked, the substitution-as-target case, ordinary deletes that must stay quiet, and the nesting and unbalanced edges.

## Note on the nightly

This came from the mutation report, and that report has now failed 14 nights running for a separate reason: the sweep is **2,520 mutants at ~0.93/min ≈ 45 hours** against a 2.8-hour budget, so it can never finish, and with `--no-shuffle` it retests the same first 4.4% every night. That is worth fixing on its own and is not part of this PR.

The nightly mutation job found four surviving mutants in `agents_ops.rs`. A surviving mutant means the line can be changed to something wrong and every test still passes, which is the same as having no test for it.

**One of the four is a real behaviour, not an adapter:**

```rust
.filter(|a| !a.starts_with("--"))
```

That `!` separates a **flag** from an **agent name**. Deleting it survived, so nothing anywhere asked what `agents disconnect --all` does. Inverted, a disconnect-everything becomes a lookup for an agent literally named `--all`, which cannot exist: the user is told no such agent was found while every agent stays wired.

The other three are the public lines-only entry points. Mutants returning `vec![]`, `vec![String::new()]` and `Default::default()` all survived, because nothing called them and looked at the result. They are thin, and thin is exactly where this happens: a one-line delegation reads as too obvious to test right up until it delegates to the wrong thing.

| mutant | result with the new tests |
|---|---|
| delete the `!` | **FAILS** |
| `run` -> `vec![]` | **FAILS** |
| `run_outcome` -> `Default::default()` | **FAILS** |
| `run_with_guard_bin` -> `vec![String::new()]` | **FAILS** |
| restored | 22 pass |

The name-that-does-not-exist test is there so the `--all` assertion cannot pass on a function that ignores its argument entirely.

Closes DD audit **D16**.

## What was there

Nothing. No tarpaulin, no codecov, no llvm-cov, no job in any workflow. Mutation
testing existed but covered `agent-guard` alone and gated nothing — so `cli`,
holding the updater, the release verifier and 16.8k lines, had no instrumentation
at all.

That is the crate whose defects replace the binary a user is running. On
2026-08-21 one of them did.

## The floor is measured, not chosen

Ran it. **79.42%**, 10,722 of 13,500 lines. Floor at **75**.

Roughly four points of headroom, about 540 lines going untested before it fires.
A gate set at today's exact number fires on the first refactor that moves a line,
and a gate that fires on noise is one people learn to force through.

## The distribution says where the risk is

```
 64.43%  4161 lines  cli            <- the updater and release verifier
 84.88%  7838 lines  agent-guard
 88.76%   881 lines  dashboard-kit
 96.98%   431 lines  graph
 99.44%   177 lines  notify
100.00%    12 lines  safe-io
```

`cli` is both the weakest and the one that matters most — the average hides that,
which is why the breakdown is written into the config rather than left in a CI
log.

**A per-crate floor is deliberately NOT set here.** Any meaningful value fails
this build today. That is a change to make with tests, not with a config line,
and it is recorded rather than left for somebody to discover later.

## Consistency with the paid repo

The `llvm` engine, matching it. The ptrace engine reports differently on the same
tree, and two repos measuring the same thing differently is how a number stops
meaning anything across the seam.

Verified locally **with the committed config** before pushing: 79.42%, exit 0.

candidates.body:
Spec 052, the Community half. Passed adversarial review after one fix round: 17 mutations applied, 15 caught, and the group half was run **on Linux** because macOS cannot see it.

## The defect

Install the paid product on a stock Ubuntu and the dashboard home page errors. The agent runs with `ProtectHome=yes`, so `/home` is **empty in its mount namespace** and no `chmod` or ACL can ever make the guardrail's file readable. This has never worked on any standard Ubuntu.

The shared data moves out of the home. **The hardening stays**: the right answer is not to need it relaxed.

## An environment variable is not a fix

The free CLI is run by three things: the operator in a shell, hooks inside AI agents that inherit the agent's environment, and the MCP proxy launched by an MCP client. A variable in `/etc/profile.d` covers the first and misses the two that generate the decisions that matter.

Resolution order, working with **no environment variable**:

1. `IW_GRAPH_FILE`
2. `/etc/innerwarden/guard.toml`, world-readable, the path only
3. `$HOME`, unchanged

With no Active Defence installed nothing changes: the free product alone writes to the home, which is where it belongs.

## Hostile input

`guard.toml` is written by the other product's installer and read as untrusted input. Symlink, FIFO, directory, group-or-world-writable, unreadable, oversized, non-UTF-8, not TOML, empty, padded, over-long, control characters, relative, `..`: each falls back to `$HOME` **and reports the problem**. Never a silent fallback, because a silent one puts the free CLI's writes and the paid agent's reads on two different files, which is the defect being fixed.

Absoluteness is tested as "starts with `/`", not `Path::is_absolute`, which is false for `/var/...` on Windows and would make the rule mean two different things.

## The finding that mattered

The first round set the new file to 0660 and called it done. **Measured on test001, Ubuntu 24.04:**

```
dir 0770 test001:adm  -> new file lands test001:test001
dir 2770 test001:adm  -> new file lands test001:adm
```

Linux gives a new file the **creator's** primary group unless the directory is setgid. So with `/var/lib/innerwarden/guard` at 0770 `innerwarden:innerwarden` exactly as the spec describes, the file lands `<operator>:<operator group>` and user `innerwarden` falls into **other, with zero bits**. Same `graph_absent` symptom. Half a fix that looks complete, which is the exact pattern this spec exists to end.

The writer now sets the new file's **group** to the directory's group as well as its mode, so the free half is correct whatever the installer does.

## The other four findings

- the "exactly one resolver" pin only covered the file that was never broken; it now walks the crate. A second resolver really existed, in `record_health`, reporting health on a file in the home while every write went elsewhere.
- the "never a silent fallback" guarantee was unpinned at the shipped call site, twice.
- the group-writable test only covered **world**-writable, because the fixture used 0666 which trips both bits.
- a doc comment that contradicted itself after the edit.

candidates.body:
fix(guard): record suppression changes, the one thing the guard did silently

`guard-events.jsonl` carried a `guard.blocked` line for every refusal and nothing
at all for the refusals being switched off. `innerwarden allow` wrote
`suppress.toml` and the event stream did not move.

Found by dogfooding: the guard blocked this agent five times in two days and every
block is in the file with a risk score and a reason. Then the agent ran
`innerwarden allow` for one command, and the sink's mtime stayed at the previous
block while `suppress.toml` gained an entry. The action that changes what the guard
will stop in FUTURE was the only action it did not report.

That is a blind spot exactly where an attacker aims first, and it matters more here
than in most places: `guard-events.jsonl` is documented as the sink a co-located
Active Defence agent tails and ingests as incidents. A guardrail being weakened is
precisely the thing that pipeline should see, and it could not.

`guard.suppression_changed` now records the action, the pattern, and the resulting
counts for all three lists, so a reader can reconstruct the posture in force at any
moment rather than only the deltas it happened to catch.

Written in `save()` rather than in the `cmd_*` handlers. Every mutation reaches disk
through that one function, so a future subcommand cannot add a suppression path and
forget to report it — the property is structural, not a convention.

Details worth stating:

  * Removals are recorded too. A stream carrying only additions cannot reconstruct
    what was actually in force.
  * `--list` writes nothing and therefore reports nothing. A stream that fires on
    reads trains its reader to ignore it.
  * The pattern is redacted before it is written: a command glob can carry a secret.
  * Emission is best-effort and cannot fail the write it reports on, matching
    `emit_guard_event`.

Existing consumers are unaffected: the Active Defence ingester filters on
`kind == "guard.blocked"` and skips everything else, with a test asserting it. Making
that pipeline raise an incident on this new kind is a separate change in that repo.

Verified end to end with the built binary against a temp config, not only through the
pure delta helper: `allow` emits `allow_added` with `allow_count: 1`, and
`allow --remove` emits `allow_removed` with `allow_count: 0`.

- **Scope: gate for the accelerator, not for the primary mechanism.** This issue's parent

  serialization for its primary, committed scope — deterministic replay-to-instant serves

  not" — this rewrite is that re-scoping. `part_of_feature: 363` is unchanged: this task is not
  wasted, deferred, or closed, it still tracks real, wanted work, and #333 (FEAT-056)'s
  checkpoint child (#839) still consumes it as-is.
- **Non-vacuity: the mutation-testing ratchet already in the tree, not a hand-rolled null.**
  `docs/mutation-testing-trial-2026-07.md` §6 is an **Adopt** verdict, and `pom.xml`'s `pitest`
  profile already lists `jls.sim.*` in `targetClasses` with an `80` `mutationThreshold` that may
  only move up. A committed codec variant that omits one field by hand is one mutant in a repo
  that already generates hundreds weekly over the exact package the codec lands in. **P3's
  committed null is deleted.** Non-vacuity comes from the ratchet instead, falling back to a
  `@ParameterizedTest` driven off #426's own field map (its § Internal interfaces provided —
  public / P5 deliverable) if bytecode mutators prove too coarse for "field omitted from
  serialization" specifically.
- **Fixtures: the existing golden corpus, not six new committed `.jls` files.** The project
  already builds circuits as text at test time — `test/jls/ElementSimulationGoldenTest.java`'s
  `CircuitTextBuilder` and its reflective `COVERED`/`EXEMPT` element-vocabulary ratchet — and has
  moved away from hand-maintained fixture files for exactly this reason. **P5's six committed
  `.jls` fixtures, and their per-fixture reachability proofs, are deleted.** The round-trip
  property runs parameterized over the same in-code corpus and the same reflective sweep instead;
  a format epoch cannot neuter a circuit built from a string at test time.
- **Cadence: checkpoint every event boundary over a short run, not a hand-tuned cadence.** "State
  that exists only between events" (the original framing for why six purpose-built fixtures were
  needed) is wrong: every field this task cares about — `Register.toBeValue`, a queued
  `MemoryWrite`, `StateMachine.busy`, `WireNet.conflictReported`, clock phase, a `TestGen`
  cursor — is set on one event and cleared on a later one, i.e. a **window** spanning multiple
  event boundaries, not an instant between them. Checkpointing at every boundary over a
  short, existing golden run hits every window by construction; short-and-dense beats
  long-and-sparse on coverage per second. The cadence/coverage tradeoff (former H4, Open
  Question 1) is dropped as unnecessary.

  function of state. Two assertions are added before anything else runs:

  codec produces false failures an executor would misdiagnose as codec bugs — exactly the
  misattribution this issue's own O2 (below) already spends a section preventing for a different
  cause.
- **Retirement sequence is the primary second observable; the VCD tail is a corollary.** VCD
  carries only watched signals at timescale resolution — a lossy projection that can miss the
  same-time reorderings it exists to catch. `Simulator.afterEvent(SimEvent)` is the seam
  `BatchSimulator` already uses for trace accumulation; comparing `(time, seq, element id,
  payload kind)` at every retirement catches every same-time reordering exactly and reports the
  divergence in the vocabulary it actually occurred in.

This rewrite adopts that direction in place — same issue, same designator, narrower and better-sequenced scope. No new issues are filed; the six duplicate slices already closed against this issue (#661, #663, #664, #667, #669, #670) stay closed here. ## Abstract At `2d0ca9d` the macOS and Windows build jobs exist and run the full suite, but both carry a job-wide `continue-on-error: true`, macOS never passes `-Djls.test.headless=false` so its 25 display-tagged classes self-skip, and both install their HDL simulators best-effort with an `exit 0` / `::notice` fallback that silently drops the HDL-gated tests. ## Proposed disposition

The adversarial review (verdict: needs-rework) found that this issue's governing citation — `docs/parity-contract.md`, which § 1 (Capability Statement & Scope Boundary) told implementers "do not restate it; implement it" — has never existed on any branch reachable from this checkout, and that the evidence commit and `docs/plan/**` corpus everything else was pinned against are likewise unreachable. It also found the machine-readable `blocks` list and mermaid graph stale against a mirror correction recorded only in a comment, an IC-1 null test loose enough to pass on one trivial fault, an unexercised `UNKNOWN` verdict, and a tension between "not one line of `jls.sim`" and retirement-indexed input logging that the issue never resolves.

The visionary review (verdict: endorse-with-reframing) found that the differential-oracle capability this issue proposes to build **already exists** in `riscv/` (`verify.py`, `fuzz_diff.py`, `riscv_ref.py`) and is simply never run in CI — the single highest-leverage action available costs a CI job, not sixteen maintainer-weeks. It endorses the null test, `UNKNOWN`-is-never-`PASS`, and retirement indexing outright, and reframes everything else: the deliverable is a documented trace format and a comparator program, not an in-jar Java record type and a behavioral CPU package; the field list should adopt the RISC-V ecosystem's own RVFI/Spike-commit-log shape rather than invent one; boot-length comparison needs a streaming digest plus bisection, not two materialized whole traces; and the exclusion set should start capped at zero.

Per process this issue is not being closed, merged, or split to enact either recommendation. The body below **is** the redirected scope: the adversarial review's factual defects are fixed in place (evidence re-pinned to a commit that actually exists, the `blocks`/`serves_capstones` machine block re-verified against every issue it names today, IC-1 tightened, an `UNKNOWN` criterion added, the retirement-counting seam named explicitly), and the visionary review's reframings are folded in as the feature's actual design: CI wiring of the existing `riscv/` oracle is phase 0, the null test reuses the project's already-adopted PIT apparatus, the RVFI-shaped trace format replaces the bespoke Java record, the comparator is a small program over a digest-plus-bisect strategy, and the exclusion set ships at cap zero. One further correction, found independently while re-verifying this issue's own dependents rather than by either review: `serves_capstones` named four capstones, but #295 has since closed `not_planned`, and both #304 and #306 have since redirected their own required-feature sets to drop this feature entirely (§ Recorded decision context) — only #301 still requires it, and `serves_capstones` is corrected to match.

## Abstract

A drawn structural circuit and an independent reference are compared per **retired instruction** rather than per cycle, over a trace format this issue specifies as a document (not a Java type), so a fast implementation and a slow one can be held to the same answer without being held to the same microarchitecture or the same language. A knowingly-wrong implementation must be rejected before a green run means anything. The project's only existing differential oracle for this exact machine class (`riscv/verify.py`, `riscv/fuzz_diff.py`) already exists and already does most of this at final-state granularity — it is simply never invoked in CI. This feature's first, near-zero-cost act is to run it; everything that follows narrows the failure it cannot yet localize (which instruction, which field) without paying for infrastructure a real boot-length run cannot afford to materialize in full.

## Intended Audience & Impact

- **Anyone who claims a drawn CPU "booted Linux".** The claim becomes checkable. A transcript alone proves the transcript; a per-retirement comparison against an independent reference proves the machine.
- **A student verifying a design they did not write.** A differential oracle reporting the exact retirement index and field that diverged, not "the run failed".
- **The ternary machine (#345)**, whose emulator has no external reference at all — its record projection is this comparator's second consumer, once #345 has a funded beneficiary again (it currently does not; see Related issues).
- **A grader** (#369). Grading reports are this comparator's output rendered for a course.
- **A reviewer reading a green check.** The null test (IC-1) means the check has been observed failing at least once. That is the difference between evidence and an unexamined assumption.

No single child asserts this alone: a trace format without a comparator compares nothing; a comparator without the null test converts an assumption into a green check.
