candidates.body:
A build of `develop` (ee817ef) on Gradle 9.8.2 ends with "Deprecated Gradle features were used in this build, making it incompatible with Gradle 10." Three uses are behind it:

1. `build.gradle:4`, in `buildscript { repositories { maven { ... } } }`: `url projectRepositoriesMavenUrl`, the space-assignment syntax of the Groovy DSL, which Gradle 10 removes. `gradle/repositories.gradle:15` already writes `url = "$projectRepositoriesSnapshotsRepoUrl"`.
2. `gradle/libs.versions.toml:64`: the plugin ID `com.github.ben-manes.versions` of gradle-versions-plugin 0.67.0, which the plugin itself reports as deprecated in favour of `io.github.ben-manes.versions`.
3. `Configuration.setVisible(boolean)`, called by gradle-pitest-plugin 1.19.0 (`info.solidsoft.gradle.pitest.PitestPlugin.createConfiguration`, `PitestPlugin.groovy:103` in the stack trace), removed in Gradle 11. 1.19.0 is the plugin's latest release (2026-03-29), and its `master` still sets `configuration.visible = false` (`PitestPlugin.groovy:112`, 2026-11-06), so this one cannot be fixed here.

## Reproduction

On `develop` at ee817ef, in a copy made with `git archive`, JDK 25.0.5+8:

```shell
$ ./gradlew --no-daemon --no-configuration-cache --warning-mode all build --dry-run
Build file '.../build.gradle': line 4
Properties should be assigned using the 'propName = value' syntax. Setting a property via the Gradle-generated 'propName value' or 'propName(value)' syntax in Groovy DSL has been deprecated. This is scheduled to be removed in Gradle 10. Use assignment ('url = <value>') instead. Consult the upgrading guide for further information: https://docs.gradle.org/9.8.2/userguide/upgrading_version_8.html#groovy_space_assignment_syntax
The com.github.ben-manes.versions plugin id is deprecated; apply io.github.ben-manes.versions instead.
The Configuration.setVisible(boolean) method has been deprecated. This is scheduled to be removed in Gradle 11. Consult the upgrading guide for further information: https://docs.gradle.org/9.8.2/userguide/upgrading_version_9.html#deprecate-visible-property
$ ./gradlew --no-daemon --no-configuration-cache --warning-mode all --stacktrace help | grep -A4 'setVisible(boolean) method'
...
	at info.solidsoft.gradle.pitest.PitestPlugin$_createConfiguration_closure2.doCall$original(PitestPlugin.groovy:103)
```

## Precedent

- The Gradle upgrading guides linked in the two messages above; `gradle/repositories.gradle:15` of this repository uses the assignment form already.
- The plugin's own message for the ID; its 0.67.0 is the release this build pins (`gradle/libs.versions.toml:7`, released 2026-10-31). In the family, astrapi69/comparator-extensions applies `io.github.ben-manes.versions` at the same 0.67.0 (`gradle/libs.versions.toml:37` on its `develop`, since its #12), as do crypt-api, checksum-up and swing-base-components.

## For 29.2

Decided by the maintainer's rule of 2026-11-05: improvements, documentation additions and edge cases without a broken contract go into the next minor.

1. `build.gradle:4`: `url = projectRepositoriesMavenUrl`.
2. `gradle/libs.versions.toml:64`: `id = "io.github.ben-manes.versions"`, the same version; `./gradlew dependencyUpdates` still runs.
3. gradle-pitest-plugin: nothing to change here until a release stops calling `setVisible`; the next update of the catalog checks the message again. Gradle 11 is the deadline, not 10.
4. Check: `--warning-mode all build --dry-run` prints only the third message.

## Does it break callers?

No. Build scripts and a plugin ID; nothing that is published changes.

Found while fixing #95 (PR #101), recorded for 29.2 in the findings of 2026-11-05; checked again on `develop` at ee817ef.

candidates.body:
file-worker, a test dependency, depends on silly-collection at runtime: file-worker 18.0 on 28.1, directly and through silly-strings 9.2; file-worker 19.1 on 28.1; file-worker 20.0 on 28.2. Gradle resolves coordinates equal to the project's own to the project itself, so the project's own jar was on `testRuntimeClasspath`, beside `build/classes/java/main` and without a task dependency on `:jar`: `test` needed `mustRunAfter(jar)`, and `./gradlew build pitest` failed Gradle's validation. The pull request of #36 excludes the project's own module from `testRuntimeClasspath` (`gradle/dependencies.gradle`). That removes the symptom, not the cycle.

## What the tests use

- From file-worker, once the tests of #36 write into `@TempDir` (no `DeleteFileExtensions` any more): only `PathFinder.getProjectDirectory` and `PathFinder.getRelativePath`, in `MigrateToTomlVersions`, a test class whose only test prints two paths and asserts nothing.
- From silly-io: `StringOutputStream`, in `PropertiesExtensionsTest`.

## Checked: silly-io 5.0 as the only test dependency

silly-io has no runtime dependencies (5.0, and 3.6 as well), so it brings nothing back. But silly-io 5.0 is built for Java 25 (class file version 69, `org.gradle.jvm.version` 25 in its module metadata), and this project compiles and tests with Java 17. Gradle refuses it; in a throwaway project with a Java 17 toolchain and `testImplementation 'io.github.astrapi69:silly-io:5.0'`:

> Dependency resolution is looking for a library compatible with JVM runtime version 17, but 'io.github.astrapi69:silly-io:5.0' is only compatible with JVM runtime version 25 or newer.

The same holds for file-worker 20.0. silly-io 3.6 is the last release for Java 17 (class file version 61); it has no runtime dependencies either, and it contains `StringOutputStream`. So silly-io 5.0 becomes possible only when silly-collection moves to Java 25, a major release, as silly-io 4.0 did.

## Proposal, on Java 17

1. `MigrateToTomlVersions`: the JDK instead of `PathFinder` (`Path.of("").toAbsolutePath()`), or remove the class, which tests nothing.
2. Drop file-worker from the test dependencies. silly-io 3.6 is then the only family library for IO in the tests.
3. Remove the exclude from `gradle/dependencies.gradle`, and check with `./gradlew dependencies --configuration testRuntimeClasspath` that silly-collection does not appear.

None of the other dependencies leads back to silly-collection: the test dependencies test-object 9 and 9.1 and vintage-time 6 have no dependencies, nor have the runtime dependencies jobj-core 9.1 and silly-bean 3.0; comparator-extensions 2 depends on commons-collections4 only (their POMs on Maven Central).

The family's rule since 2026-10-30 (astrapi69/mystic-crypt#235, in mystic-crypt's `.claude/rules/library-first.md`): every library of the family compiles, tests and releases on JDK 25; one on an older version moves at its next release, as a new major version with a CHANGELOG sentence on the new minimum. silly-collection is on JDK 17 (`projectSourceCompatibility=17`; `java-version: '17'` in `gradle.yml` and `publish.yml`), so its next release is 29.0, as silly-io moved with 4.0 (astrapi69/silly-io#14).

## To do

- `projectSourceCompatibility=25` in `gradle.properties`, `java-version: '25'` in `.github/workflows/gradle.yml` and `.github/workflows/publish.yml`.
- Gradle 9: the build is on Gradle 9 already (9.7.0 on develop, 9.8.2 with #50). Check that the JDK 25 toolchain resolves in CI and that PIT with `pitest-junit5-plugin` runs on it, with the score and the floor of #36.
- The pins of #49 go: `gradle/version-catalog-update.gradle` pins silly-io and file-worker to 3.6 and 19.1, their last releases for Java 17. On JDK 25 the catalog takes silly-io 5.0.
- The only family library for IO in the tests is silly-io 5.0, which has no runtime dependencies. file-worker goes: its only use left, `PathFinder` in `MigrateToTomlVersions`, a class that asserts nothing, is replaced by the JDK or removed. With it go the path back to silly-collection and the exclude of `testRuntimeClasspath`, and #37 is done.
- The CHANGELOG of 29.0: the sentence on the new minimum. The fixes of #39 to #46 bring the code in line with its name and its Javadoc, so they are bug fixes and go into 28.3, before this release.

## The family repositories below JDK 25 that use silly-collection

Gradle refuses a library built for Java 25 on the class path of a project below 25 (as it refuses silly-io 5.0 here, see #37), so each of these stays on 28.x until it moves to JDK 25 itself, at its next release by the same rule. Found by GitHub code search on the default branches on 2026-11-04 (`io.github.astrapi69:silly-collection` in the version catalog or the build files), with the version each declares:

candidates.body:
29.0 and 29.1 had every line covered and 99% of PIT's mutants detected, and the parameterized tables of #92 still found eleven defects (#113 to #118, #126, #127, and #138, #141, #143, #145 for 29.2). Coverage says that a line ran; the mutation score says that the tests notice a small change of the code that is there. Neither says that the tests ask for what the name, the Javadoc or the implemented interface promise.

## What the two numbers did not see, with the cases of 29.1

- **Inputs no test used.** PIT changes the code, not the inputs: the overflow of `newRangeArray` at `Integer.MAX_VALUE` (#113), a collection with a repeated key in `mergeAndSummarize` (#116), a null element in `getFirst`/`getLast`, `ArrayIterator` and `SetEnumeration` (#114, #118, #126).
- **Tests that pinned the wrong behaviour.** The old `ArrayIterator.remove` tests expected the broken result (#118); every mutant that changed it was "detected".
- **Weak assertions.** The tests of `newLinkedHashMap` of pairs compared maps with `equals`, which ignores the order, so the lost order of the pairs (#115) passed.
- **Missing code.** `InsertionOrderMap` did not override `putAll` (#127); PIT mutates what is there, so there was no mutant to survive.
- **Not code.** silly-bean declared for the runtime only (#95) is build metadata.
- **PIT's `DEFAULTS` mutators** change conditions, boundaries and return values, not the order of a data structure or an overflow path.

## Proposed, for 29.2 (one pull request per point)

1. **Contract test suites for the collection classes.** The interfaces they implement already have test suites:
   - Apache Commons Collections 4.6.0, a dependency of this library, publishes its tests as `commons-collections4-4.6.0-tests.jar` (on Central): `AbstractListTest`, `AbstractSetTest`, `AbstractMapTest`, on JUnit 5 (checked in the 4.6.0 tests jar). Commons tests its own `SetUniqueList` (`SetUniqueListTest extends AbstractListTest`), `ListOrderedSet` and `ListOrderedMap` with them.
   - Guava's `guava-testlib` 33.8.0-jre: `ListTestSuiteBuilder`, `SetTestSuiteBuilder`, `MapTestSuiteBuilder` generate the cases of the `List`, `Set` and `Map` contracts per feature (`CollectionFeature.ALLOWS_NULL_VALUES`, `KNOWN_ORDER`, ...); Guava tests its own collections with them. They build JUnit 3 `TestSuite`s, so they need the JUnit Vintage engine.
   - Candidates: `UniqueList`, `SortedList`, `SortedUniqueList` (with their documented refusals as unsupported features), `InsertionOrderSet`, `IndexableSet`, `InsertionOrderMap`, `ArrayIterator` (`IteratorTester` of guava-testlib). Commons first, as the family rule takes an existing dependency before a new one; guava-testlib where Commons has no suite, such as the iterator.
2. **Generated inputs.** Property-based tests with jqwik 1.10.2 (a JUnit Platform engine; it generates edge cases such as `Integer.MAX_VALUE`, empty and null first, and shrinks a failing case) for the factories and extensions of `array`, `list` and `map`: e.g. "`newRangeArray(start, end)` has `end - start + 1` elements, the first `start`, the last `end`". The family's `randomizer` gives random values, but no edge-case generation and no shrinking; say in the pull request why it does not fit, or use it where plain random values are enough.
3. **Stronger mutators.** PIT's `STRONGER` group in addition to `DEFAULTS` (removes conditionals, more return values); measure the CI time and the new survivors first, then decide on the floor.
4. **A rule for the test rows**, in the README's Contributing and the agents' briefs: the rows come from the Javadoc and the interface's contract, not from what the code does; for each method one row per promise, and one each for null, empty, the boundary, a duplicate and the order where it applies.

Tests and build only; no change to `src/main` beyond what a suite shows to be a defect (those go into their own issues, by the triage rule).



## Best practice (added on 2026-11-08, rule AG-114)

- Martin Fowler, "Test Coverage" (17 April 2012, https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TestCoverage.html): "Test coverage is a useful tool for finding untested parts of a codebase. Test coverage is of little use as a numeric statement of how good your tests are."
- PIT, "Basic concepts" (https://pitest.org/quickstart/basic_concepts/): "An effective set of tests should fail in the presence of the mutant", and mutants that cannot be told apart are "equivalent mutations": a mutation score measures the tests against the code that is there, not against the contract.
- Contract suites test the contract itself: Apache Commons Collections tests its own `SetUniqueList` with `SetUniqueListTest extends AbstractListTest` (commons-collections4 4.6.0 `-tests.jar`), and `ListOrderedSet` and `ListOrderedMap` with `AbstractSetTest` and `AbstractOrderedMapTest`.

Closes #98.

## What was wrong

PIT ran inside `gradle.yml`: the job `build` ran `./gradlew build` and then `./gradlew pitest`, and `make pitest` ran PIT on the local machine. Several local PIT runs at the same time crashed the maintainer's machine on 2026-11-05. Mutation tests run on GitHub only from now on, as in astrapi69/comparator-extensions since #33 (PR #34), whose files this pull request takes over.

## Commits, each green on its own

1. `build: mutation testing runs on GitHub, in a workflow of its own, with a summary and the report (#98)`: the workflow, the summary script, the move out of `gradle.yml`, the two Makefile targets, the README and the comments that named `gradle.yml` for PIT.

No test commit comes first: a workflow, a Makefile target and a README have no unit test. What shows the change works is the run of the new workflow on this pull request and the `make pitest` dispatch on its branch, both under "Verified".

## The change

- **`.github/workflows/mutation-testing.yml`**, "Mutation testing", job `pitest`: on a push to `develop` or `master`, on a pull request against them, and on demand (`gh workflow run mutation-testing.yml --ref <branch>`). It runs `./gradlew pitest`, which fails below `mutationThreshold = 95` (build.gradle), writes a summary of the run into the job summary and the log, and keeps PIT's report (HTML and `mutations.xml`) as the artifact `pitest-report`. A newer push to a pull request cancels its running mutation test; on `develop` and `master` every push runs, as each publishes its badge.
- **`.github/scripts/mutation-summary.py`**: killed of total, the score as PIT rounds it, the floor read from build.gradle, and every mutant not detected (class, method, line, mutator, status); also on a red run, as PIT writes its report before it checks the floor.
- **Moved out of `gradle.yml`, unchanged but for the job they hang on**: the step "Mutation testing", the mutation context step (awesome-well-tested's converter, the same pinned commit) and its artifact `mutation-context`, the step "Mutation score badge" with the hand-over artifact `badges`, and the job `publish-badges`, which now `needs: pitest`. The badge files are the same, `badges/mutation-score-develop.json` and `-master.json` on `gh-pages`, so the README badge keeps working.
- **`gradle.yml`** keeps what it did beyond PIT: `./gradlew build` (tests, JaCoCo with its floors, javadoc with `-Werror`, Spotless) and the codecov upload. Its permissions comment now points to `mutation-testing.yml`.
- **Makefile** (as comparator-extensions#28, PR #47): `make pitest` runs no PIT locally. It refuses a detached HEAD and a branch whose HEAD is not `origin/<branch>` ("push it first"), starts the workflow for the current branch, and prints the run's URL, `gh run watch <id>`, `make pitest-status` and how to download `pitest-report`; it does not wait. `make pitest-status` shows the newest "Mutation testing" run of the current branch, whatever started it, and once it is complete the `## Mutation testing` block of its log.
- **README**: "Releasing" step 3 drops `pitest` from the local gate. PIT's numbers and floor come from the "Mutation testing" run on the release pull request, and again from its run on the merge commit, whose tree is the tag's tree. The GitHub release links that run, with the proof that the trees match (`git rev-parse "<the run's commit>^{tree}" "RELEASE-X.Y^{tree}"`). The gate also runs with an empty local Maven repository, as `gradle/repositories.gradle` reads `mavenLocal()` before Central; the rest of step 3, javadoc with `-Werror` from #97 included, is kept. Step 4 tags once the run on the merge commit has the numbers of the gate. "Contributing" says how to run PIT (`make pitest`, `make pitest-status`, the artifact). The Quality section says which workflow runs what.
- The comments in `build.gradle`, `gradle/mutation-testing.gradle` and `.github/scripts/mutation-score-badge.py` that named `gradle.yml` for PIT now name `mutation-testing.yml`.

The family catalog lists no script that writes a PIT summary; it covers `scripts/` directories, not `.github/scripts`. comparator-extensions' `.github/scripts/mutation-summary.py` (#33) is the model the issue names. silly-strings has a variant (#59), but it does not read the floor, which the issue asks for. The comparator script is taken over with the two changes below.

Callers: none. No class of the library changes; nothing a consumer compiles against or runs is touched. awesome-well-tested finds the workflow that enforces the floor by looking for the PIT call in every workflow (`scripts/verify_repo.py`), so its next check of `develop` will find `mutation-testing.yml` and the artifact `mutation-context` there.

## Proposed in review

- **The summary holds the score at 99 while a mutant survives**, as PIT does when it checks `mutationThreshold` (`PercentageCalculator.getPercentage(long, long, int)` of PIT 1.30.1, read from its bytecode: half up, then `min(score, 100 - 1)` unless every mutant is detected) and as `mutation-score-badge.py` already does. comparator-extensions' script rounds 999 of 1000 to 100%. For this repository's 971 mutants the two agree, but the summary should not show a score PIT never reports.
- **Class and method in backticks** in the summary table, as silly-strings' summary has them. The job summary is Markdown, and a constructor's `<init>` would be dropped as an unknown HTML tag. With no floor in build.gradle the line says "the floor is not set", where comparator's printed "not set%".
- **The GitHub release (step 6) carries the link** to the run on the merge commit, with the tree proof. The CHANGELOG entry is written before the merge, so it cannot link a run of the merge commit.
- The Quality section says "A pull request into `develop` is merged only when both are green", as comparator-extensions' does. It holds once the branch protection names the checks (see "Verified" for their names).

Closes #135.

Why: Gradle 9.8.2 ends the build with "Deprecated Gradle features were used in this build, making it incompatible with Gradle 10." Three uses are behind it. This PR removes the two that are ours; the third stays (see below).

1. `build.gradle:4`: `url projectRepositoriesMavenUrl` becomes `url = projectRepositoriesMavenUrl` (as `gradle/repositories.gradle:15` has it).
2. `gradle/libs.versions.toml:64`: plugin id `com.github.ben-manes.versions` becomes `io.github.ben-manes.versions`, same version 0.67.0 (as comparator-extensions, crypt-api, checksum-up and swing-base-components).

Commit: one, build files only (a deprecation of the build cannot be pinned by a test row; the pin is the warning output).

Evidence, `./gradlew --no-daemon --no-configuration-cache --warning-mode all build --dry-run`:

```
before (develop 9959eb2):
Build file '.../build.gradle': line 4
Properties should be assigned using the 'propName = value' syntax. [...] scheduled to be removed in Gradle 10. [...]
The com.github.ben-manes.versions plugin id is deprecated; apply io.github.ben-manes.versions instead.
The Configuration.setVisible(boolean) method has been deprecated. This is scheduled to be removed in Gradle 11. [...]

after (this branch):
The Configuration.setVisible(boolean) method has been deprecated. This is scheduled to be removed in Gradle 11. [...]
```

Only the third message is left, as the issue's check says. `./gradlew --no-daemon dependencyUpdates` still runs (BUILD SUCCESSFUL, tasks `partialDependencyUpdates` and `dependencyUpdates`). `./gradlew --no-daemon clean spotlessCheck build`: BUILD SUCCESSFUL.

Third deprecation, `Configuration.setVisible(boolean)` from gradle-pitest-plugin 1.19.0: left as it is, no plugin version is added here. Finding for the coordinator (checked in the plugin's repository, szpak/gradle-pitest-plugin):
- 1.19.0 (2026-03-29) is still the latest release; it sets `configuration.visible = false` unconditionally.
- It is fixed on the default branch, unreleased: `CHANGELOG.md` "1.20.0 - Unreleased": "Fix Gradle 9 deprecation warnings - PR #398", commits `fa4297b22` (2026-03-31), `ea38ebfa8` (2026-04-01, "Use dynamic call for better compatibility"); `PitestPlugin.groovy` there guards the call with `if (GradleVersion.current() < GradleVersion.version("9.0"))`. So the issue's statement that its `master` still sets `configuration.visible = false` unconditionally does not hold for today's master (last commit 2026-10-27); it needs a release (1.20.0) first. Nothing to upgrade to yet; the next catalog update checks the message again. Gradle 11 is the deadline.

Callers in the family: none; build scripts and a plugin id, nothing published changes. `git grep ben-manes` finds the id only in the catalog (CHANGELOG lines are history of old versions).

Proposed in review: none beyond the above; the third deprecation is left for a decision once gradle-pitest-plugin releases.

Closes #51. Builds on #82 (`29.0-SNAPSHOT`), whose commit it holds until #82 is merged; both change neighbouring lines of `gradle.properties`.

## What changes

By the family's rule since 2026-10-30 (astrapi69/mystic-crypt#235), every library compiles, tests and releases on JDK 25, and one on an older version moves at its next release as a new major version.

- `projectSourceCompatibility=25`: the toolchain compiles and tests with Java 25; the class files are of major version 69.
- `java-version: '25'` in `gradle.yml`, `publish.yml` and `dependency-submission.yml`.
- silly-io 5.0 in the tests, its release for Java 25. The pin of `gradle/version-catalog-update.gradle` to 3.6 goes with its reason (#37). silly-io has no runtime dependencies, so nothing leads back to silly-collection: `testRuntimeClasspath` holds silly-io 5.0 and no silly-collection.
- PIT 1.30.1, as silly-io uses on JDK 25; `pitest-junit5-plugin` 1.2.3 runs on it.
- The CHANGELOG draft of 29.0, under BREAKING: Java 25 is the minimum; a project below 25 stays on 28.3 until it moves itself; the projects of the family it concerns are listed on #51. The README's Releasing section names JDK 25 and major version 69 for the gate.

The runtime dependencies jobj-core 9.1, silly-bean 3.0 and comparator-extensions 2 are their latest releases, built for Java 17, and work on 25 as they are. The published POM keeps them as runtime dependencies.

## Verified

- `./gradlew clean spotlessCheck build pitest jacocoTestReport javadoc --no-build-cache` with the Java 25 toolchain (Temurin 25.0.4): green, with the numbers of 28.3's release gate: 518 tests in 24 classes, 0 failures, 3 skipped; PIT 781 of 794, floor 95; JaCoCo 1247 of 1247 lines and 546 of 558 branches, floors 98 % and 95 %; no javadoc warning.
- `UniqueList.class`: major version 69.
- `./gradlew dependencies --configuration testRuntimeClasspath`: `io.github.astrapi69:silly-io:5.0`, no silly-collection.

Closes #36.

#49 builds on this branch: the dependencies raised with versionCatalogUpdate. Merge this one first.

## Score

| | mutants killed | score |
|---|---|---|
| develop `ae86f5b`, before | 625 of 721 | 87% |
| this branch | 703 of 721 | **97.5%** (PIT shows 98%) |

PIT 1.30.0 with its default mutators, through `info.solidsoft.pitest` 1.19.0 and `pitest-junit5-plugin` 1.2.3, JDK 17. The floor is `mutationThreshold = 95` in `build.gradle`, 85 before: the measured score minus about two points, rounded down. PIT rounds the score half up to a whole percent before it compares, so with the 721 mutants of today the build fails from 40 survivors on. JaCoCo: 1146 of 1146 lines, before as after; 474 of 488 branches, 464 before.

| classes | killed before | killed now |
|---|---|---|
| `UniqueList`, `SortedList`, `SortedUniqueList` | 18 of 43 | 40 of 43 |
| `ListExtensions`, `ListFactory`, `VectorExtensions`, `CollectionExtensions`, `ArrayExtensions`, `ArrayFactory` | 386 of 416 | 409 of 416 |
| `MapFactory`, `MapExtensions`, `InsertionOrderMap`, `SetFactory`, `IndexableSet`, `InsertionOrderSet`, `SetExtensions` | 95 of 121 | 114 of 121 |
| `IndexSortedProperties`, `SortedProperties`, `PropertiesExtensions` | 74 of 89 | 88 of 89 |
| the other classes | 52 of 52 | 52 of 52 |

## The 18 survivors

| mutant | why no test kills it |
|---|---|
| `UniqueList.add:78`, `SortedList.add:112`: replaced boolean return with true | both return what `ArrayList.add(E)` returns, which is always true |
| `SortedList.add:117`: replaced boolean return with true | it returns whether the size changed, which it always has once `add(int, E)` returns |
| `SetFactory.newHashSet:77`, `newInsertionOrderSet:145`, `newLinkedHashSet:190`, `newTreeSet:242`: changed conditional boundary of `0 < elements.length` | `Collections.addAll` with an empty array adds nothing, to a set no caller has seen yet |
| `CollectionExtensions.containsAtLeastOne:69`, `ListFactory.newCharacterArrayList:427`, `ArrayFactory.newByteArray:137`: the same boundary | an empty array changes nothing either way |
| `ListExtensions.relocate:523`: changed conditional boundary | at `newIndex == size()`, `add(e)` and `add(size(), e)` both append |
| `IndexableSet.get:58`: both mutants of the range check | the check only ends the loop early, before the same exception |
| `IndexSortedProperties.removeKey:283` (private): removed call to `resortKeyList` | taking one key out of a sorted index leaves it sorted; only the constructor case of #45 could observe the call |
| `InsertionOrderSet.add:134`: replaced boolean return with true | the method returns true also for an element the set holds: #41 |
| `ListExtensions.removeLastValues:618`: changed conditional boundary | the method removes the first values, and its check throws where its own message says it should not: #43 |
| `ArrayExtensions.concatenate:164`, `CollectionExtensions.toList:254`: removed conditional | both return their argument itself, which their Javadoc contradicts: #47 |

14 are equivalent; 4 wait for the decision of their issue.

## What changed

Eight commits, each green on its own (`./gradlew spotlessCheck build` on every one):

1. `build(test)`: the test runtime class path no longer holds this project's own jar. file-worker 18.0 depends on silly-collection 28.1, directly and through silly-strings 9.2; Gradle resolves that to this project, so the jar sat on `testRuntimeClasspath` without a task dependency on `:jar`, and `./gradlew build pitest` failed Gradle's validation. `testRuntimeClasspath` excludes the project's own module, and the `mustRunAfter(jar)` of `test` is gone with its cause, as in silly-io. The cycle itself is #37.
2. to 6. `test`, by area: what the tests check, in their commit messages. No change to `src/main`.
7. `docs(changelog)`: 28.2 was released, but its section was still headed 28.2-SNAPSHOT, and the entry of #31 sat in it; that entry now opens the section of 28.3-SNAPSHOT.
8. `build`: the floor, the badge, the README badge, `make pitest`, the CHANGELOG.

**No `refactor` commit.** The redundant code considered for removal sat in public methods (`SortedList.add`, the four `SetFactory` factories, `containsAtLeastOne`, `newByteArray(int...)`, `newCharacterArrayList`), so it stays, and its mutants are among the equivalent ones above.

**Every new or changed test kills a mutant or covers a case no test covered before.** Checked with one PIT run with `fullMutationMatrix = true` (not committed), against the baseline report:

- 77 of the 78 newly detected mutants are killed by a named new or changed test; the 78th, `ListExtensions.computeAllCombinations:121`, which only weakens a pruning, times out under `testGetAllCombinationsWithSizeOfAllValues`.
- The new tests that kill nothing that survived before cover a branch JaCoCo reported missed before: `testNewByteArrayWithIntArrayNull` (`ArrayFactory:137`), `testContainsAtLeastOneWithoutObjects` (`CollectionExtensions:69`), `testNewCharacterArrayListWithoutCharacters` (`ListFactory:427`, two branches), `testGetKeyFromValueWithEmptyMap` (`MapExtensions:74`), `testClearWhenEmpty` (`IndexSortedProperties:162`); or a case no test had: `testGetKeysFromValueWithoutMatch` (a value no entry holds) and `testGetThrowIndexOutOfBoundsExceptionAtSize` (the index equal to the size of a set that is not empty; the old tests used size + 1 and the empty set, where the check in the loop is never reached).
- Changed tests without a new kill: the sort tests of `MapExtensions` now compare the order of the keys, which `assertEquals` of two maps ignored; `SortedUniqueListTest.testAddAll` builds the class it is named for; the `@TempDir` rewrites of `PropertiesExtensionsTest` keep what they check.
- No test pins an implementation detail: the type checks in `MapFactoryTest` check the type the `@return` of each factory names; the three `subList` tests are characterizations, Javadoc and all, that pin a modifiable list of its own, the only thing that tells it from

The release 29.0: `projectVersion=29.0`, the CHANGELOG entry that replaces the 29.0-SNAPSHOT draft, and the README for 29.0.

The release carries milestone 29.0 (#51, #77, #78, #87, all closed) and the README of #85:

- **BREAKING:** Java 25 (#51). The sorted lists with a comparator refuse explicit positioning, as `TreeSet` does: `set`, `sort`, `addFirst`, `addLast` and the `set` and `add` of their list iterators throw `UnsupportedOperationException`; `replaceAll` writes only values that keep the order; the algorithms of `Collections` that write through `set` throw at their first write and leave the list unchanged (#77, #78, #87). `subList` of the three list classes and `reversed()` of the sorted lists read and remove only (#78, #87). `UniqueList.reversed()` refuses the two moves its view cannot make keep their contract (#77).
- **FIXED:** `UniqueList.reversed()` adds at the index of the view (#77); `SortedUniqueList.set` without a comparator swaps (#77); `UniqueList.addFirst`/`addLast` move a held element (#87); `setComparator` keeps comparator and order when its sort throws (#87); `SortedList.addAll` of the list itself (#77).
- **MIGRATION FROM 28.x:** for each breaking change what it was, what it is and what to change.
- **README:** installation 29.0 (28.3 for Java 17); "Upgrading from 28.x": 28.3 is the last release for Java 17, the 28.x line is frozen but for security fixes, which come as a patch on a branch `release/28.x` from `RELEASE-28.3`; new fixes and features in 29.x only. Quality with the numbers of the gate below.

Open issues before the cut: #92, of milestone 29.1 (parameterized tests); milestone 29.0 has none open.

## Gate

On the tree of the head of this pull request, `7a9bf03` (tree `3b150bba55256e0217b4b64cc39522c08d922c0d`), the same code as `develop` 9fc046e: JDK 25 toolchain (Temurin 25.0.4), `--no-daemon`: `./gradlew clean spotlessCheck build pitest jacocoTestReport jacocoTestCoverageVerification javadoc --rerun-tasks --no-build-cache`.

| check | result |
|---|---|
| tests | 640 in 25 classes, 0 failures, 3 skipped |
| `pitest`, floor 95 | passed: 960 of 971 (98.9%); the 11 survivors are equivalent |
| `jacocoTestCoverageVerification`, floors 0.98 / 0.95 | passed: 1502 of 1502 lines, 611 of 622 branches |
| `javadoc` | no warning |

The gate runs again on the tree of the merge commit before the tag, with the class files (major version 69) and the resolved tree (no SNAPSHOT).

## After the merge

`RELEASE-29.0` is tagged on the merge commit of this pull request with `./gradlew tagRelease` once its tree is the gate's, and pushed; `publish.yml` uploads to the Central Portal, where the deployment waits for the maintainer (`USER_MANAGED`).

`scripts/check-reproducible.sh` pinned the JDK of its two builds with `-Porg.gradle.java.installations.{auto-detect,auto-download,paths}`, as project properties. Gradle 9.8.2 reports each as deprecated, scheduled for removal in Gradle 10 ("Instead, specify it as a Gradle property", upgrading guide 9, "toolchain-project-properties"); with Gradle 10 the pin would no longer hold and the builds could run on any JDK Gradle detects. The script runs Gradle with `-q`, so its own output never showed the warnings. This pull request passes the three as Gradle properties (`-D`), with the same lines and comment as astrapi69/jobj-core#56, the precedent, whose script came from here.

Measured on Temurin 25.0.5+8 (the JDK `.sdkmanrc` names) with Gradle 9.8.2, `./gradlew --no-daemon --warning-mode all javaToolchains` with the three settings, each run from an empty configuration cache:

| form | toolchain deprecation warnings | JDKs listed |
|---|---|---|
| `-P` (before) | 3 | 1, the pinned one |
| `-D` (this pull request) | 0 | 1, the pinned one, detected by the Gradle property `org.gradle.java.installations.paths` |

The configuration cache is on in `gradle.properties`: a `-D` run right after the `-P` run reused its entry and never configured the project, so the `-D` row is from a run after `.gradle/configuration-cache` was removed. Both runs also print one deprecation of the pitest plugin (`Configuration.setVisible(boolean)`, scheduled for removal in Gradle 11), which this pull request does not touch.

`scripts/check-reproducible.sh ~/.sdkman/candidates/java/25.0.5.0+8-tem` with `-D`: "identical, 5 artifacts", exit 0.

Closes #203

No mutation testing ran here; the coverage figure (98.08 %) was the only statement about the tests, and awesome-well-tested lists the repository as Bronze for that reason.

- `gradle/libs.versions.toml`: pitest 1.30.0, JUnit 5 plugin 1.2.3, Gradle plugin 1.19.0.
- `gradle/mutation-testing.gradle` (in `gradle-files.list`; `/gradle` is in `.gitignore`, the file is force-added like the other gradle files): targets `io.github.astrapi69.collection.*`, `mutators = ["DEFAULTS"]` named explicitly, HTML and XML reports.
- `build.gradle`: `pitest { mutationThreshold = 85 }`, where the list's check reads it.
- `.github/workflows/gradle.yml`: `./gradlew pitest` after the build, then the list's converter (pinned to commit `3d1258d`) writes `mutation-context.json` and the run keeps it as the artifact `mutation-context`.

Measured locally on 2026-10-17:

```
>> Generated 721 mutations Killed 625 (87%)
total 721, killed 625, survived 94, no coverage 2, timed out 0
tool_score 0.8669, strict_score 0.8669, test_strength 0.8693
```

The floor of 85 leaves a margin of twelve mutants; 80 would leave about fifty. Ninety-four survivors are the next step; the list's Gold needs the floor and a green run, which this gives.

**Read before merging.** The local `develop` this branch was cut from is three commits ahead of `origin/develop`, all yours, all from 2026-08-24 and never pushed: "build: migrate to Gradle 9.7.0 and Central Portal publishing", "release version 28.2", "created a new 28.3-SNAPSHOT version". They are in this branch, so the PR shows four commits. Pushing `develop` first (`git push origin develop` from your clone) shrinks the PR to the one commit above; merging as is brings them in through the PR. The PIT wiring was measured on the migrated build, so it is not rebased onto the older `origin/develop`.

**Second commit, found by this PR's first CI run.** `gradle/tagging.gradle` is applied by `gradle-files.list` since the migration commit, but `/gradle` is in `.gitignore` and the file was never force-added, so a fresh clone fails with "Could not read script gradle/tagging.gradle" (CI did, 2026-10-17). Closes #45.

**Builds on #59** (#46: the key set view and the transient comparator). Merge #59 first. Until then this pull request also shows its two commits; its own are the last two.

As decided on #45, the index follows the `Properties` contract. It holds exactly the keys that `get` and `keySet` give: the keys of the object's own entries, not those of its defaults, sorted with the comparator, independent of swing-table-components.

## What was wrong

The cases of #45, each run against the head of #59:

| case | before | now |
|---|---|---|
| `put("A", "1")`, then `put("A", "2")` | `get(0)` and `get(1)` both "2": the key is indexed twice | "2", `null` |
| then `remove("A")` and `put("B", "3")` | `get(0)` null, `get(1)` "3", `indexOf("3")` 1 | "3", `null`, 0 |
| defaults A=1, B=2, then `put("C", "3")`, or else `putAll({C=3})` | index `[1, 2, 3]` after `put`, `[3]` after `putAll` | `[3]` after both |
| `putIfAbsent`, `merge`, `compute` | not in the index | in the index; a remapping to null takes the key out |
| `computeIfAbsent`, `computeIfPresent` to null | the added key is missing, the removed key stays | the index follows both |
| `load` of a key that is twice in the input | indexed twice | once |
| `copy = orig.clone()`, then `copy.setProperty("B", "2")`, `copy.remove("A")` | `orig.get(0)` null, `orig.indexOf("1")` -1 | "1", 0: the copy has an index of its own |
| `get(-1)`, `getProperty(-1)`, `remove(-1)` | `IndexOutOfBoundsException` | `null`, as their Javadoc says |
| a subclass whose `newComparator()` returns a comparator from one of its fields | the constructor calls `newComparator()` before the field is set | the constructor does not call it; the first read of the index does |

## The two commits

1. `test: pin what IndexSortedProperties does today (#45)`: tests that assert today's results in these cases, each green and with a Javadoc line that names #45. No change to `src/main`.
2. `fix: the index of IndexSortedProperties holds exactly the keys of its entries (#45)`: the fix. The tests of the first commit now assert the correct results.

## What the fix does

- The index is built from the keys when it is read. `sortedKeys()` takes them from `keys()`, sorted, and keeps them until the keys change.
- Each method of the class that may change the keys drops the index: `put`, `putAll`, `putIfAbsent`, `remove(Object)`, `remove(Object, Object)`, `clear`, `compute`, `computeIfAbsent`, `computeIfPresent`, `merge`. `setProperty` and `load` go through `put`, and the key set of #46 goes through `remove(Object)` and `clear()`.
- `entrySet()` and `values()` remove entries without a method of this class, but cannot add any. So an index of another size than the object is built again as well (`testRemoveThroughEntrySetAndValues`). This goes beyond the list of the decision, so that the index holds the keys after every change.
- `replace` and `replaceAll` change values only (`testReplaceAndReplaceAll`).
- The list of the index is replaced, never changed in place. So a clone, which starts with the list of the original, has an index of its own. The index is `transient`, being built from the keys.
- `get(int)`, `getProperty(int)` and `remove(int)` check `0 <= index`. `getProperty(int)` is `synchronized` now, since it may build the index.
- The constructor no longer touches the index, and so no longer calls `newComparator()`.
- The class Javadoc says what the index holds.

**Existing tests changed.** Ten tests of `IndexSortedPropertiesTest` expected the keys of the defaults in the index: `testConstructor`, `testConstructorSortsTheKeysOfTheDefaults`, `testGetInt`, `testGetPropertyInt`, `testIndexOf`, `testClear`, `testFactoryMethods`, `testFactoryMethodsWithComparator`, `testOfWithComparatorSortsTheIndexWithIt` and `testOfWithComparatorAndNullIsGreaterThan`.
- They now check that the index does not hold those keys. Where they check the index, they put their entries into the object with `putAll`.
- `testConstructorSortsTheKeysOfTheDefaults` is renamed `testConstructorLeavesTheKeysOfTheDefaultsOutOfTheIndex`, since the constructor no longer does what the old name says.

**The one caller in the family:** swing-table-components' `PropertiesTableModel` (see the comment on #45).
- Its `getRowCount()` is `data.size()`, which never counted the defaults. A model built from `Properties` reads its rows through an index that now holds the same keys that `size()` counts.

## Verified

- `./gradlew spotlessCheck build` on each of the two commits: green.
- `./gradlew build pitest --no-build-cache`: PIT kills **714 of 731** mutants (97.7%). That is 715 of 733 on #59 and 703 of 721 on develop.
- All 99 mutants of the properties classes are killed. The 17 survivors are those of develop, without `IndexSortedProperties.removeKey:283`, which is gone with the method.
- A first version of `sortedKeys()` had one equivalent survivor: the null check of `keys == null || ...`, forced so that the index is always built again (the same index, only slower). The check is now written so that every mutant of it changes a result.

Closes #75.

## What was wrong

`ArrayFactory.newBooleanArray`, `newByteArray(byte...)`, `newCharArray`, `newDoubleArray`, `newFloatArray`, `newIntArray`, `newLongArray` and `newShortArray` returned the array they were given: `int[] a = {1, 2}; ArrayFactory.newIntArray(a) == a` was `true`, and a write to the result changed the caller's array. Their Javadoc promised "the new array". It is the fault of #62 for the primitive types; `newByteArray(int...)` built a new array already.

## Two commits, each green on its own

1. `test: pin what the factory methods of the primitive types return today (#75)`: `testNewPrimitiveArrayWithGivenArray` pins the identity with `assertSame` for each of the eight, `testNewPrimitiveArrayWithNull` pins what stays: null gives null. No change to `src/main`.
2. `fix: the factory methods of the primitive types return a new array (#75)`: the fix, below.

## The fix

As decided for #62, each of the eight returns `elements == null ? null : elements.clone()`. The Javadoc says that the result is a new array, also when no elements are given, and that null gives null. `testNewPrimitiveArrayWithGivenArray` now asserts a new array with the same values for each of the eight. No other test changed.

Callers in the family (`file-worker`, `mystic-crypt`, `crypt-data`, `swing-table-components`, all in tests) pass their values as varargs, so the copy cannot be noticed.

## Verified

- `./gradlew spotlessCheck build`: green on each commit; 464 tests (develop: 462).
- `./gradlew build pitest --no-build-cache`: PIT kills **725 of 738** mutants (develop: 717 of 730). The eight conditionals add one mutant each, killed by `testNewPrimitiveArrayWithNull`; the existing tests kill the eight "replaced return value with null". The 13 survivors are those of develop, none in changed code; the one of `newByteArray(int...)` moved to line 146.
- `./gradlew javadoc`: no warning.
- Touches other methods of `ArrayFactory` than #71 (#62); `git merge-tree` with it: no conflict.

Closes #35.

Stacked on #48: this pull request targets `build/mutation-testing`, so that its diff shows its own commit only. Merge #48 into `develop` first; GitHub then retargets this one to `develop`, and its CI build runs (the workflow runs for pull requests into `develop` and `master` only).

## What versionCatalogUpdate raised

| dependency | from | to |
|---|---|---|
| commons-collections4 (runtime) | 4.5.0-M2 | **4.6.0**, a release instead of the milestone on the consumers' class path (#35) |
| junit-jupiter, junit-jupiter-params | 5.11.3 | 6.1.3 |
| mockito-core | 5.14.2 | 5.24.0 |
| test-object | 9 | 9.1 |
| plugin spotless | 8.10.0 | 8.11.0 |
| plugin versions | 0.61.0 | 0.67.0 |
| plugin version-catalog-update | 1.1.1 | 1.1.2 |
| silly-io | 3.2 | 3.6, not 5.0 |
| file-worker | 18.0 | 19.1, not 20.0 |

commons-collections4 4.6.0 keeps commons-codec optional, as 4.5.0-M2 did: the consumers get no new runtime dependency.

## silly-io and file-worker

versionCatalogUpdate raised them to 5.0 and 20.0. Both are built for Java 25 (`org.gradle.jvm.version` 25 in their module metadata), and this project compiles and tests with Java 17, so Gradle refuses them:

> Dependency resolution is looking for a library compatible with JVM runtime version 17, but 'io.github.astrapi69:silly-io:5.0' is only compatible with JVM runtime version 25 or newer.

They go to their last releases for Java 17, silly-io 3.6 and file-worker 19.1 (module metadata: `org.gradle.jvm.version` 17), and `gradle/version-catalog-update.gradle` pins both, with that reason in a comment. A second run of `./gradlew versionCatalogUpdate` leaves the catalog unchanged. Its report lists the two pinned updates with a wrong version reference ("silly-io (comparator-extensions) 3.6 -> 2"), the same with `pin { versions = [...] }`; the pins work all the same. The cycle through file-worker is #37.

## Verified

- On this branch: `./gradlew spotlessCheck build pitest --no-build-cache`, green; PIT kills 703 of 721 mutants, as on #48 without the raise.
- With the same raise on `develop`'s tests (before #48): `./gradlew build` green, PIT 625 of 721, as before the raise.

candidates.body:
Closes #41.

## What was wrong

- `InsertionOrderSet.add` was `super.remove(o); return super.add(o);`. After the remove the set never holds the element, so `super.add` always returned `true`. `add("a")` twice on a new set returned `true` the second time. Its own Javadoc says `@return true if the set did not already contain the specified element`, and `LinkedHashSet` returns `false`.
- `addAll` is inherited from `AbstractCollection` and calls `add` for each element. It returned `true` for any non-empty collection: `addAll(List.of("a"))` on a set that holds "a" returned `true`.
- `IndexableSet` extends `InsertionOrderSet` and inherits both.
- `IndexableSet.getIndex` called `entry.equals(element)` and threw a `NullPointerException` as soon as its loop reached a `null` element. For a set of `null` and "a", `getIndex("a")` threw instead of giving 1.

## Commit 1: `test: pin what InsertionOrderSet.add and IndexableSet.getIndex do today (#41)`

Five tests assert today's results and pass on `develop`. The Javadoc of each names #41 and says that the fix changes the result.
- `InsertionOrderSetTest`: `add("a")` on a set of a and b returns `true`, and a moves to the end; `addAll([a])` on a set that holds a returns `true`.
- `IndexableSetTest`: the same two cases for the inherited `add` and `addAll`; and for a set of `null` and "a", `getIndex("a")` and `getIndex(null)` throw a `NullPointerException`.

## Commit 2: the fix

- `add` keeps the result of `super.remove(o)`, which says whether the set held the element, and returns its negation. The issue says the result has to come from the remove. A held element still moves to the end, as the class Javadoc says.
- `addAll` needs no change of its own. It now returns `true` when at least one element was new, as `Set.addAll` says.
- `getIndex` compares with `Objects.equals`.

The tests of commit 1 now assert `false` for a held element in `add` and in `addAll`, and 1 and 0 for `getIndex("a")` and `getIndex(null)`. The `getIndex` test also checks -1 for an element the set does not hold. A new test shows that `addAll` with a new and a held element returns `true` and orders both as the collection does. No existing test pinned the old results, and none changed.

## Verified

- `./gradlew spotlessCheck build pitest --no-build-cache`: green on both commits. On the fix, PIT kills 704 of 721 mutants (`develop`: 703 of 721).
- The survivor "replaced boolean return with true" of `InsertionOrderSet.add`, named in the issue, is killed. So is every other mutant of `add` and `getIndex`.
- The two survivors left in `IndexableSet` are in `get`, which this pull request does not change.

candidates.body:
Closes #76.

## What was wrong

- `ArrayExtensions.removeFromStart(array, prefix)` and `removeFromEnd(array, suffix)` used only the length of the prefix or suffix: `removeFromStart({1, 2, 3}, {9})` gave `{2, 3}`, `removeFromEnd({1, 2, 3}, {9})` gave `{1, 2}`. Their Javadoc says "Removes the given prefix array".
- A prefix or suffix longer than the array threw an undocumented `NegativeArraySizeException`.
- `removeFromStart` of an empty array returned the given array itself, of a non-empty one a new array.
- `removeFromEnd` checked no argument: null threw a `NullPointerException`, where `removeFromStart` throws an `IllegalArgumentException` through `Argument.notNull`.
- `remove({0, 1, 2, 3}, -1, 2)` threw "Index -1 out of bounds for length 3" for an array of length 4: it checked each index against the list after the removals before it.

## Two commits, each green on its own

1. `test: pin what removeFromStart, removeFromEnd and the message of remove do today (#76)`: five tests in `ArrayExtensionsTest` pin the results above, each with a Javadoc line saying that the fix of #76 changes it; `testRemoveFromStartAndEndWithTheWholeArrayAndWithNullElements` pins what stays (a prefix or suffix as long as the array gives an empty array, a matching null element is removed). No change to `src/main`.
2. `fix: ...`: the fix, below.

## The fix

- Both methods remove the prefix or suffix only when the array starts or ends with it, compared element by element with `Objects.equals` (`Arrays.equals` over the range), so null elements match. Otherwise, also for a longer prefix or suffix, they return a copy of the given array, as `StringUtils.removeStart` and `removeEnd` of Apache Commons Lang do for strings.
- The result is always a new array of the component type of the given array (`Arrays.copyOfRange`, `Arrays.copyOf`, `clone`), as #62 decided for the factories and #64 for the component type.
- Both check their arguments with `Argument.notNull`: null throws an `IllegalArgumentException`.
- `remove` checks every distinct index with `Objects.checkIndex` against the length of the given array before it removes any, so the message names that length.
- The Javadoc of the three says all of this. The five tests of the first commit now assert these results; the one with a prefix that does not match also checks a prefix and a suffix that match in part only. No other test changed.

Callers in the family: none. mystic-crypt's `CryptObjectDecoratorExtensions` has private `byte[]` methods of the same names.

## Verified

- `./gradlew spotlessCheck build`: green on each commit; 486 tests (develop ba67302: 480).
- `./gradlew build pitest --no-build-cache`: PIT kills **724 of 737** mutants (develop: 721 of 734). Every mutant of `remove`, `removeFromStart` and `removeFromEnd` is killed; the 13 survivors are those of develop.
- `./gradlew javadoc`: no warning.

Closes #43.

## What was wrong

- `removeLastValues([A, B, C, D, E, F], 2)` returned `[C, D, E, F]`. By its name and its Javadoc it returns `[A, B, C, D]`.
- `removeLastValues(list, list.size())` threw an `IllegalArgumentException`, whose message says that it is thrown for more values than the list holds. Six is not more than six. PIT counted the boundary mutant of this check as a survivor.
- `sortByProperty([obelix, asterix, miraculix], Person::getName, true)` sorted descending, `[obelix, miraculix, asterix]`; its Javadoc says "if true the sort will be ascending otherwise descending". `false` sorted ascending.

## Two commits, each green on its own

1. `test: pin what removeLastValues and sortByProperty do today (#43)`: four tests in `ListExtensionsTest` pin the faulty results, each with a Javadoc line saying that the fix of #43 changes the result: `testRemoveLastValuesResult` (`[C, D, E, F]`), `testRemoveLastValuesWithSize` (the exception), `testSortByPropertyWithAscendingTrue` (descending) and `testSortByPropertyWithAscendingFalse` (ascending). No change to `src/main`.
2. `fix: ...`: the fix, described below.

## The fix

- `removeLastValues` returns `v.subList(0, v.size() - remove)` for `remove <= v.size()`: `[A, B, C, D]` for the case above, and an empty list for `remove == size()`. Only `remove > size()` throws, with the same message as before. The result is a `subList` of the given list, as before. The Javadoc now says what the method returns and names the exception.
- `sortByProperty` reverses the comparator for `ascending == false` instead of `true`. A null value comes first in the ascending order and last in the descending one.

The four tests of the first commit now assert the documented results.

**Existing test changed:** `ListExtensionsTest.testSortByProperty` asserted the inverted order in all three of its blocks, under its comments "ascending" and "descending". The blocks now assert the order their comments name: ascending `[asterix, miraculix, obelix]`, descending `[obelix, miraculix, asterix]`, and ascending with the name of asterix null `[asterix, miraculix, obelix]`, the null first. `testRemoveLastValues` (the size of the result) and `testRemoveLastValuesException` (7 of 6 throws) stay as they are and pass.

No other repository of the family calls either method; see the comment on #43.

## Verified

- `./gradlew spotlessCheck build`: green on each commit; 394 tests on the branch, 390 before.
- `./gradlew build pitest --no-build-cache`: PIT kills **705 of 722** mutants (develop: 703 of 721). The first commit alone gives 704 of 721: `testRemoveLastValuesWithSize` kills the boundary mutant of `removeLastValues:618`. The fix adds one mutant, the subtraction in `v.size() - remove`. All six mutants of the two methods are killed. 17 survive: the 18 of develop without `removeLastValues:618`, none of them in the changed code.
- `./gradlew javadoc`: no warning.
- Merges with #55 (#40, the other change to `ListExtensions`) without a conflict: `git merge-tree` of the two branches.

candidates.body:
Closes #42.

## What was wrong

`CollectionExtensions.isEqualCollection` ended with

```java
return retainAll.isEmpty() || one.containsAll(other) && other.containsAll(one);
```

The first operand made two collections of the same size without a common element equal, and nothing compared the cardinality. On develop `f2ddea9`:

| call | develop | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| `isEqualCollection([1, 2], [3, 4])` | `true` | `false` |
| `isEqualCollection([1, 1, 2], [1, 2, 2])` | `true` | `false` |
| `[{"1", "23", "3"}, {"4", "25", "9"}]` and `[{"x"}, {"y"}]` (lists of `String[]`) | `true` | `false` |

## The two commits

1. `test: pin what isEqualCollection does today (#42)`: three new tests in `CollectionExtensionsTest`, one per case above, assert today's result, `true`. The Javadoc of each names #42 and says that its fix changes the result to `false`. No change to `src/main`.
2. `fix: isEqualCollection compares the elements and their cardinality (#42)`: the method keeps its handling of null and of different sizes (`preconditionOfEqualCollection`) and then returns `CollectionUtils.isEqualCollection` of commons-collections4, which is already a dependency. It returns true exactly when both collections hold equal elements with the same cardinality, whatever their order. Its Javadoc now says that, and that the elements compare by `equals`, so arrays compare by identity. The three tests of commit 1 now assert `false`. Two new tests: `testIsEqualCollectionComparesArraysByIdentity` (the same arrays in another order are equal; other arrays with the same content are not) and `testIsEqualCollectionWithSameElementsInAnotherOrder` (`[1, 1, 2]` and `[2, 1, 1]` are equal).

## Existing tests that relied on the bug

- `CollectionExtensionsTest.testEqualCollections` compared two lists of different `String[]` arrays with the same content and expected `true`. Arrays compare by identity, so it passed only because the lists had no common element. The test is named for equal collections, so its lines are now `List<String>`, which compare by content. That arrays compare by identity is checked by the new test.
- `ListExtensionsTest.testGetCombinations`: `getCombinations([1, 2, 3, 4], 3)` returns each combination in reversed order, `[[3, 2, 1], [4, 2, 1], [4, 3, 1], [4, 3, 2]]`, and `[1..7]` choose 6 does the same. The old comparison let this pass. The Javadoc of `getCombinations` ("Gets all possible combinations from the given list") promises no order within a combination, so `getCombinations` is unchanged, and the test sorts each combination before comparing. The outer comparison still uses `isEqualCollection`, so each combination must appear exactly once.

The tests in other repositories that rely on the bug (json-extensions, gson-extensions, csv-worker; listed in the comment on #42) are not touched here.

## Verification

- `./gradlew spotlessCheck build` is green on each of the two commits.
- `./gradlew spotlessCheck build pitest --no-build-cache` on this branch: PIT kills **701 of 719** mutants (97.5%; the floor is 95). Develop: 703 of 721. The old last line had two more mutants, and both were killed. Every mutant of `isEqualCollection` and `preconditionOfEqualCollection` is killed. The size check in the precondition is now redundant for `isEqualCollection`, but `testIsEqualListOfArrays` still kills its mutant. The 18 survivors are the same as on develop; none is in the changed code.

Closes #179.

## Why
Tests hold the inputs their author thought of; #113 (overflow at `Integer.MAX_VALUE`) and #116 (a key that appears n times counted 2n - 1 times) lay in inputs no test used. Decided by the maintainer on 2026-11-11: option 2, no new library. The tests now generate their inputs from one shared source and check a property that the Javadoc promises. Test code only, `src/main` is unchanged.

## Commits
1. `test: a shared source of edge-case inputs for the parameterized tests (#179)`: `EdgeCases` next to `Elements` (`@MethodSource` factories: the nine `int` edge cases of jqwik's user guide, "Generation of Edge Cases", string collections (empty, one element, null, a duplicate, the reversed order), pairs of ints for ranges, seeds and `java.util.Random`), with `EdgeCasesTest`.
2. `test: properties of the array, list and map factories and extensions over the edge cases (#179)`: `ArrayPropertiesTest`, `ListPropertiesTest`, `MapPropertiesTest`; each test's Javadoc quotes the Javadoc sentence it checks.

## Evidence
- Each commit green with `./gradlew --no-daemon clean spotlessCheck build`.
- Tests (sum of `tests` in `build/test-results/test/*.xml`, 3 skipped before and after): develop 2029, after commit 1 2038, after commit 2 3936 (+1907: 9 in `EdgeCasesTest`, 1194 `ArrayPropertiesTest`, 406 `ListPropertiesTest`, 298 `MapPropertiesTest`).
- PIT, read from the CI logs (`gh run view <id> --log | grep ">> Generated"`): the run on this PR (43170304272, head 53edf79) `>> Generated 1347 mutations Killed 1315 (98%)`, line coverage of the mutated classes 1601/1601, test strength 98%; the last develop run (43169956092, 5655986) the same, `>> Generated 1347 mutations Killed 1315 (98%)`. The mutants are of `src/main`, which this PR does not change, so the numbers are equal. All checks on the head are green (build, pitest, codecov patch and project, GitGuardian, Socket).
- No property failed, so no defect: nothing is left out ("Not yet included: defects found" is empty).

## Properties added
Array: `newRangeArray` (length, first, last, consecutive, for the short edge ranges and for random ranges from a seed; throws for more than `Integer.MAX_VALUE` numbers and for end < start), `newSubArray`, `newArray` (copy, existing array plus elements), `remove`, `removeFirst`/`removeLast`, `removeFromStart`/`removeFromEnd`, `intersection`, `toSet`, `splitInChunks`. List: `newArrayList`/`newLinkedList`/`newVector` (also with a collection), `newUniqueList`, `newRangeList`, `revertOrder`, `toIndexMap`, `removeFirst`/`removeLast`, `toArray`, and the same answer for a list and an array from `getFirst`, `getLast`, `isFirst`, `isLast`, `indexOf`/`hasNext`/`hasPrevious`, `getNextElement`/`getPreviousElement`, `getFirstElement`/`getLastElement` (the documented null difference included). Map: `mergeAndSummarize` (1 to 3 repetitions, any order from a seed, a key the map does not hold with and without fullMerge), `getKeyFromValue`, `getKeysFromValue`, `valuesAsList`, `swap`. `MapFactory`'s `KeyValuePair` methods are not tested: they leave the API in 30.0 (#158).

## Why no randomizer
The family's randomizer 10.7 (latest release) depends on `io.github.astrapi69:silly-collection` 28.1 (checked in its pom on Central), which would put an old copy of this very library on its own test classpath. The JDK's `java.util.Random` with a fixed seed (shown in the test name, so a failure can be rerun) is enough (RL-098 takes the JDK first anyway). No new dependency at all.

## CHANGELOG
No bullet: test code only, nothing a caller notices (DC-007).

## Proposed in review
- Edge ranges of `newRangeArray` that an array can hold but the JVM cannot allocate (more than 5 numbers, at most `Integer.MAX_VALUE`) are not generated; they would end in an `OutOfMemoryError`, which the Javadoc names as the JVM's.
- `mergeAndSummarize` uses the start values of the `int` edge cases that a count of 3 can be added to; the overflow of `Integer::sum` is not promised in the Javadoc.
- The test classes are `*PropertiesTest` per package (one more file each), and the list/array comparison lives in `ListPropertiesTest`.
- No shrinking: a failing case is shown as it was generated, as the decision on #179 says.

Closes #46.

`SortedProperties` inherits the Javadoc of `keySet()` and `propertyNames()` (`{@inheritDoc}`) from `Hashtable`, `Map` and `Properties`, and `Properties` is `Serializable`. The code did not do what they say.

## What was wrong

The cases of #46, each run against develop `f2ddea9`:

- `keySet()` returned a `TreeSet` copy, not a view: after `keySet().remove("A")`, `containsKey("A")` was still `true`; the set kept the keys of the moment it was made; and `add` put a key into the copy only.
- `propertyNames()` left out the keys of the defaults: with defaults A=1, B=2 it gave `[]`, where `Properties` gives `[A, B]`.
- Neither class serialized once its comparator existed, because the default comparator is a lambda: `new IndexSortedProperties()` threw `NotSerializableException`, and so did a `SortedProperties` after a call of `keys()`.

## The two commits

1. `test: pin what SortedProperties does today (#46)`: tests that assert today's results in these cases, each green and with a Javadoc line that names #46. `testOfPropertiesComparatorOfObject`, which reads the defaults through `propertyNames()`, asserts that its loop does not run. No change to `src/main`.
2. `fix: ... (#46)`: the fix. The tests of the first commit now assert the correct results.

## What the fix does

- `keySet()` returns a view backed by the properties, as `Map.keySet` specifies. It iterates the keys in the order of the comparator, from a sorted copy taken when the iterator is created, and reflects every change. Removing a key through the set, its iterator, `removeAll`, `retainAll` or `clear` removes the entry; `add` and `addAll` throw `UnsupportedOperationException`. Each removal goes through `remove(Object)` or `clear()`, so an `IndexSortedProperties` takes the key out of its index too (`testKeySetRemoveUpdatesTheIndex`).

So it lists the keys of the defaults, and of their defaults, each key once. **Behaviour change:** as `Properties.propertyNames` specifies, it now throws a `ClassCastException` for a key that is not a String. Before, it listed such keys sorted by their string form (`testPropertyNamesWithKeysThatAreNoStrings`, pinned in the first commit).
- The comparator is `transient`. `getComparator()` creates it again with `newComparator()` when it is needed, also after a deserialization. Round trips for both classes: entries, defaults, order and index survive, and a key put into the copy is sorted with a comparator of the copy's own.
- Not changed: the order in which `store` writes the entries, which no contract promises.

Existing tests changed: only `SortedPropertiesTest.testOfPropertiesComparatorOfObject`. Its loop runs now. It asserts that the loop runs once for each of the four keys of the defaults and that `getProperty` finds a default, and it passes expected before actual.

Closes #65.

## What was wrong

Both `ListFactory.newUniqueList` methods are documented as "Factory method for create new `UniqueList`" and "`@return` the new `UniqueList` as `List`", but they built a `SortedUniqueList` without comparator. The two classes are not related (both extend `ArrayList`), and they differ in `add(int, E)`: `SortedUniqueList` ignores the index and appends, `UniqueList` inserts at the index. A caller who asked for a unique list and inserted at an index got the element at the end: `newUniqueList("b", "a").add(0, "c")` gave `[b, a, c]`.

## Two commits, each green on its own

1. `test: pin what ListFactory.newUniqueList builds today (#65)`: two tests in `ListFactoryTest` pin the faulty results, each with a Javadoc line saying that the fix of #65 changes the result: `testNewUniqueListClass` (the class is `SortedUniqueList`, from a collection, from an empty one and from elements alone, so both branches of `newUniqueList(Collection, T...)` and `newUniqueList(T...)`) and `testNewUniqueListAddWithIndex` (`add(0, c)` appends). A third, `testNewUniqueListOrder`, passes before and after the fix: the elements of the collection first, then the given elements, each once where it comes first. No change to `src/main`.
2. `fix: ListFactory.newUniqueList returns a UniqueList, as its Javadoc says (#65)`: the fix, described below.

## The fix

- `newUniqueList(Collection, T...)` builds `new UniqueList<>(collection)`, or `new UniqueList<>()` for a null or empty collection, and adds the given elements with `Collections.addAll`, as before with the other class. `newUniqueList(T...)` delegates to it, as before. The return type stays `List<T>`.
- The order of the result does not change: a `SortedUniqueList` without comparator appended, as `UniqueList.add(E)` does. What changes is the class and `add(int, E)`, which now inserts at the index, or moves an element the list holds there (#39).
- The Javadoc of both methods says that the result is a `UniqueList`, what its order is, and that a caller who wants the sorted list calls `newSortedUniqueList`.

The two pinning tests now assert `UniqueList` and the insertion at the index: `[c, b, a]`, then `add(0, a)` gives `[a, c, b]`, and `newUniqueList([b, a], c).add(1, d)` gives `[b, d, a, c]`.

**Existing tests changed:** none. `testNewUniqueListCollectionObjects` and `testNewUniqueListObjects` pass unchanged; they check sizes and positions that do not depend on the class.

**Callers in the family:** none. A `grep -rn --include=*.java` (and a grep over all file types) for `newUniqueList` over the checkouts under `~/dev/git/hub/astrapi69/` and `/run/media/astrapi69/T7_Shield/dev/git/hub/` finds it only in silly-collection's `ListFactory` and `ListFactoryTest`. So no caller casts the result to `SortedUniqueList`, calls `getComparator` or `setComparator` on it, or relies on `add(int, E)` appending. file-worker (`StorableTest`, `StoreFileExtensionsTest`) and crypt-data (`SignatureAlgorithmResolverTest`) call `newSortedUniqueList`, which is not changed.

**With #67:** the list `newUniqueList` returns is a `UniqueList`, so it also gets the `set`, `replaceAll` and list iterator of #72 once both are merged. The two branches touch different files and merge without a conflict (`git merge-tree`).

The three mutants of `newUniqueList` (the branch on `isNotEmpty` and the two empty returns) are killed. The 13 survivors are the 13 equivalent ones of develop, `ListFactory.newCharacterArrayList` now at line 438 instead of 427; none is in the changed code.

candidates.body:
Closes #40.

## What was wrong

```java
List<String> list = new SortedList<>(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER);
list.add("a");
list.add("A"); // IndexOutOfBoundsException: Index: -1, Size: 1
```

`SortedUniqueList` did the same. The cause was `ListExtensions.getIndexToInsert(List, T, Comparator)`: `Collections.binarySearch` finds "a" for "A" at index 0, `contains` compares with `equals` and returns false, and the method turned the index it had found into `-0 - 1 = -1`.

Also in the issue: `add(int, E)` and `addAll(int, Collection)` of both classes ignore the index, as the class Javadoc says of every add method, but through `{@inheritDoc}` they promised to insert "at the specified position". They accept any index, a negative one too: `new SortedList<String>().add(-1, "a")` adds "a".

## Two commits, each green on its own

1. `test: pin what getIndexToInsert does today (#40)`: three tests pin the faulty results, each with a Javadoc line saying that the fix of #40 changes the result. `getIndexToInsert(["a", "b"], "A", CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER)` returns -1, and -2 for "B"; `SortedList.add` and `SortedUniqueList.add` throw an `IndexOutOfBoundsException` for "A" and "B" and leave the list as it was. No change to `src/main`.
2. `fix: ...`: the fix, described below.

## The fix

- `getIndexToInsert` converts a negative result of `binarySearch` into the insertion point and returns a non-negative one as it is, whatever `contains` says. The new element goes in at the index of the element the comparator holds equal: `[a, b]` plus "A" and "B" gives `[A, a, B, b]`, and `add` returns true. The method also no longer runs `contains` over the list on every insertion. Its Javadoc now says that the list must be sorted in the order of the comparator, and which index the method returns.
- `SortedUniqueList` stays unique by `equals`: it asks `contains` before it asks for the index, as before. Adding "a" or "B" again returns false.
- `add(int, E)` and `addAll(int, Collection)` of both classes: the Javadoc says that the index is ignored and not checked, so that any index is accepted, a negative one too. What these methods do is unchanged. Checking the index would change what the classes document.

The three tests of the first commit now assert the right results. `testAddWithIndexOutOfRange` and `testAddAllWithIndexOutOfRange` in `SortedListTest` and `SortedUniqueListTest` add at index -1 and past the end, with and without a comparator. No other existing test pinned the old result, so none is changed.

## Verified

- `./gradlew spotlessCheck build`: green on each commit; 397 tests on the branch, 393 before.
- `./gradlew build pitest --no-build-cache`: PIT kills **704 of 722** mutants (develop: 703 of 721). The condition `indexToInsert < 0` has one mutant more than `!list.contains(element)`. All five mutants of the method are killed; the boundary one is killed by `testGetIndexToInsertWithComparatorInconsistentWithEquals`, where `binarySearch` finds index 0. The 18 survivors are those of develop, none of them in the changed code.
- `./gradlew javadoc`: no warning. The rendered pages of `add(int, E)` and `addAll(int, Collection)` say that the index is ignored.
- No other repository of the family calls `getIndexToInsert` or uses `SortedList` or `SortedUniqueList`, according to a grep of the local checkouts.

## Not in this PR

`add(E)` and `addAll(Collection)` of both classes still have `{@inheritDoc}`. In an IDE that shows `ArrayList`'s "Appends the specified element to the end of this list", which is not true with a comparator. The generated Javadoc shows no description for them.

Closes #39.

## What was wrong

`UniqueList` inherits the Javadoc of `List` through `{@inheritDoc}`, and broke it:

| call | before | now |
|---|---|---|
| `[a].addAll([a])` | `true`, the list `[a]` | `false`, the list did not change |
| `[a].addAll(1, [a])` | `true`, the list `[a]` | `false` |
| `[a].addAll(5, [b])` | `true`, the list `[a, b]` | `IndexOutOfBoundsException` "Index: 5, Size: 1", as `ArrayList` throws; the list stays `[a]` |
| `[a].addAll(5, [])` | `false` | `IndexOutOfBoundsException` "Index: 5, Size: 1" |
| `[a, b].add(2, a)` | throws "Index: 2, Size: 1", and `a` is lost: the list is `[b]` | `[b, a]` |
| `[x].addAll(0, [a, a, b])` | `[x, a, b]` | `[a, b, x]`, as `[x].addAll(0, [a, b])` gives |

Both `addAll` methods returned `true` for any non-empty collection. `add(int, E)` removed a contained element before it called `super.add(index, element)`, so an index that was valid could be out of range by then, and the exception left the element removed.

## Commit 1: `test: pin what UniqueList.addAll and add(int, E) do today (#39)`

Six tests, one for each row of the table, assert the results of the "before" column and pass on `develop`. The Javadoc of each names #39 and says that the fix changes the result.

## Commit 2: the fix

- `addAll(Collection)` appends through `add(E)` and returns `true` when one element was appended.
- `addAll(int, Collection)` checks the index as `ArrayList` does: before the list changes, and for an empty collection too. An index < 0 or > size() throws an `IndexOutOfBoundsException` with `ArrayList`'s message. It inserts the elements the list does not contain yet at the index, in the order of the collection and each once. The elements it already contains keep their positions. It returns whether an element was inserted.
- `add(int, E)` checks the index first, in the same way. It inserts a new element as `ArrayList` does. A contained element moves so that it ends at the index, or at the end of the list for the index `size()`. That is what the old code meant to do: remove, then insert. The size does not change and no element is lost.

The three methods describe this in their own Javadoc now. `add(int, E)` names the move, with the example `[a, b]` → `[b, a]` for `add(0, b)` and for `add(2, a)`. `addAll(int, Collection)` says that, unlike `add(int, E)`, it leaves a contained element where it is. A private `rangeCheckForAdd(int)` holds the shared check.

The six tests of commit 1 now assert the "now" column. Seven new tests cover:
- the moves of `add(int, E)` to the front, to the back and to the same place
- new elements at an index up to `size()`
- indexes out of range: the message, and the list unchanged, for a contained and for a new element, and for `addAll` with a negative index and an empty collection
- `addAll` at the index `size()`
- a contained element that `addAll(int, Collection)` leaves in place

No existing test pinned the old results, and none changed.

## Verified

- `./gradlew spotlessCheck build pitest --no-build-cache`: green on both commits. On the fix, PIT kills 704 of 722 mutants (`develop`: 703 of 721).
- Every mutant of the changed methods and of `rangeCheckForAdd` is killed. One survivor remains in `UniqueList`, in `add(E)`, which this pull request does not change: "replaced boolean return with true" for `return super.add(element)`. It is equivalent, because `ArrayList.add` always returns `true`.
- `./gradlew javadoc`: no warnings.

Refs #77. A follow-up to #84.

After the review of #84 the maintainer decided: a `SortedUniqueList` **without** a comparator has no order to keep and swaps in `set`, as `UniqueList` does since #67, so that `Collections.swap`, `reverse`, `shuffle` and `rotate` work on it; **with** a comparator the `IllegalArgumentException` for an element held at another index stays. #84 was merged with the test commit of this change, f633c97 `test: pin that a SortedUniqueList without comparator refuses an element held at another index in set (#77)`, which pins the refusal; this PR is the fix commit on top of `develop` (8ec8e5e, with #84 and #86).

## What was wrong

With #84, `set` of a `SortedUniqueList` threw `IllegalArgumentException` for an element held at another index, with and without a comparator. Without a comparator that broke `Collections.swap`, `reverse`, `shuffle` and `rotate` on the list, which worked in 28.3 (they call `set` with an element the list holds at another index): `[a, b, c].set(0, c)` threw where `UniqueList` gives `[c, b, a]`.

## The commits

1. f633c97 (in `develop` through #84): `testSetWithoutComparatorAndElementHeldAtAnotherIndex`, `testSetWithoutComparatorWhileAnIteratorRuns` and `testCollectionsAlgorithmsWithoutComparator` pin the refusal, each with a Javadoc line saying the fix changes the result; the block without a comparator of `testSetWithElementHeldAtAnotherIndex` moved into the first of them. Green on its own: `develop` is green with it.
2. This PR: `fix: a SortedUniqueList without comparator swaps in set, as UniqueList (#77)`.

## The fix

`SortedUniqueList.set(int index, E element)` checks the index first, as `ArrayList.set` does (its message, before anything changes, for a held element too), and looks the element up.

- **Without a comparator:** if the list holds the element at another index, the two swap: the element goes to the index, the one that was at the index goes to the other's place; otherwise the element at the index is replaced. It returns the previous element and is no structural modification (no `modCount` change): a running iterator goes on. This is `UniqueList.set`.
- **With a comparator:** unchanged from #84. An element held at another index throws `IllegalArgumentException`, list unchanged; any other is sorted in, and the removed element is put back if the comparator throws.

The Javadoc of `set` describes both cases; the class Javadoc says that a list without a comparator swaps in `set`. The list iterator's `set` and `add` still throw `UnsupportedOperationException` with and without a comparator, as #84 decided.

The three tests of f633c97 now assert the swap: `[a, b, c]` with `set(0, c)` or `set(2, a)` gives `[c, b, a]` and returns `a` or `c`; an iterator that runs goes on with `b` and `a`; `Collections.swap`, `reverse` (even and odd size), `shuffle` (against a `UniqueList` with the same seed) and `rotate` by 1, -1, 2 and 3 of six elements give the results they give on a `UniqueList`. No other test changes.

**Callers in the family:** none affected, as for #84: outside silly-collection only crypt-data and file-worker tests build a `newSortedUniqueList` (without comparator) and iterate it; none calls `set` or the `Collections` algorithms on it.

## Verified

`./gradlew --no-daemon clean spotlessCheck build pitest jacocoTestReport javadoc --no-build-cache`:

- 590 tests, green, as on `develop` (the change flips three tests, it adds none).
- PIT: **852 of 863** mutants detected; `develop` gives 850 of 861. The 31 mutants of `SortedUniqueList`, the swap among them, are all killed. The 11 survivors are the equivalent ones of `develop`, none in the changed code.
- JaCoCo: 1356 of 1356 lines, 571 of 582 branches (floors 98 % and 95 %); `develop`: 1352 of 1352, 567 of 578.
- `javadoc`: no warning.
- Public and protected signatures: unchanged.
